docs.title: 5.8 Surface Codes and Lattice Surgery
docs.text:
The surface code arranges qubits on a 2D checkerboard: data qubits sit on a grid and helper qubits between them repeatedly check the parity of their four neighbours. It only needs nearest-neighbour connections, tolerates error rates near 1%, and is the most tested code in hardware. Logical operations between surface-code patches are done by 'lattice surgery' — temporarily merging and splitting patches along their edges.

A logical parity measurement by lattice surgery. Merging two patches for d rounds measures their joint logical parity without touching the logical states directly.

Think of it like…

Picture a tiled floor where every grout junction has a sensor checking the four tiles around it; a cracked tile trips the sensors on either side, and a crack that runs all the way from one wall to the opposite wall is the only kind the sensors can't catch.

Real-world example

Corvid Quantum (fictional) plans a distance-15 logical qubit: 15² = 225 data qubits plus 224 measure qubits, 449 in total. To perform a logical CNOT between two such patches, its compiler schedules lattice surgery: merge patch A with an ancilla patch for 15 rounds to measure Z̄Z̄, split, then merge with patch B to measure X̄X̄ — about 45 code cycles, or roughly 50 µs at a 1 µs cycle.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Lay out d × d data qubits with measure qubits between them on a square grid (rotated surface code).
  2. Every cycle, each measure qubit runs four CNOT/CZ gates with its neighbours and is measured, giving X-type and Z-type parities.
  3. A decoder pairs up detection events across space and time to infer the most likely error chains.
  4. Logical X̄ and Z̄ are strings of operators running across the patch between opposite boundaries.
  5. Two patches interact by lattice surgery: merging their boundaries measures a joint logical parity; splitting restores separate patches.

Who uses it

Google Quantum AI, many superconducting start-ups, and most fault-tolerant resource estimates (including RSA-breaking estimates) assume surface codes; QEC and compiler engineers work with them daily.

Key takeaway

Memorise the rotated surface code count: d² data + (d² − 1) measure qubits = 2d² − 1 physical qubits; distance 7 = 97 (Willow used 101 including leakage-removal qubits).

Going deeper

  • Kitaev's toric code (1997) placed qubits on a torus; Bravyi & Kitaev (1998) and Dennis et al. (2002) introduced planar versions with boundaries, and Fowler et al.'s 2012 review made the surface code the default architecture.
  • Bulk stabilisers have weight 4 and boundary stabilisers weight 2; X-type and Z-type checks alternate like a chessboard, and each cycle needs four entangling layers plus measurement and reset — about 1.1 µs on Willow.
  • Lattice surgery (Horsman, Fowler, Devitt & Van Meter, 2012) replaced older defect-braiding schemes; Litinski's 'Game of Surface Codes' (2019) turned it into a tile-based compilation model used in many resource estimates.
  • Clifford operations come cheaply via lattice surgery and Pauli-frame tracking, but the T gate does not; surface-code computers need magic-state factories or cultivation, which dominate space-time cost.
  • Neutral-atom systems can move atoms to perform transversal CNOTs between surface-code patches directly, an alternative to lattice surgery demonstrated by Harvard, MIT and QuEra in 2023-2025.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming the surface code encodes many qubits per block: it stores one logical qubit per patch, which is why qLDPC codes attract interest.
  • Forgetting routing space: real layouts reserve extra patches for lattice-surgery channels and factories, often doubling the qubit count beyond 2d² per logical qubit.
  • Believing distance equals the number of errors corrected: a distance-d code corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors, so distance 7 corrects 3.

docs.title: 5.9 qLDPC Codes, Colour Codes and Newer Code Families
docs.text:
The surface code is reliable but wasteful: every logical qubit needs hundreds or thousands of physical qubits. Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes keep each check small but connect qubits over longer distances, so one block can hold many logical qubits — IBM's 'gross code' stores 12 logical qubits in 288 physical ones. Colour codes and other new families trade overhead, connectivity and easy logical gates in different ways.

Surface code vs IBM's gross code for 12 logical qubits

Rotated surface code (×12) Gross code [[144,12,12]] Distance 12 12 Physical qubits ≈ 3,400 (12 × 287) 288 (144 data + 144 check) Check weight 4 6 Connectivity Nearest-neighbour grid Degree 6, some long-range Decoder Matching (MWPM) BP-based (e.g. Relay-BP) Logical gates Mature lattice surgery Needs extra modules

qLDPC codes cut qubit counts roughly tenfold but demand longer-range connections and new decoders.

Think of it like…

The surface code is like giving each passenger a private car with a driver; a qLDPC code is a well-planned bus route — far fewer vehicles for the same passengers, but you need longer roads (long-range wiring) to make it work.

Real-world example

Helix Analytics (fictional) compares storing 12 logical qubits at distance 12. Twelve rotated surface-code patches need about 12 × 287 ≈ 3,400 physical qubits on a simple grid, while one [[144,12,12]] gross-code block needs 144 data plus 144 check qubits — 288 in total — but each qubit must connect to six others, some far apart. The team picks hardware based on which wiring it can actually build.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start from classical LDPC ideas: many sparse parity checks, each touching only a few bits.
  2. Build quantum versions (hypergraph product, bivariate bicycle, lifted-product codes) whose X and Z checks commute.
  3. Map the check graph onto hardware: long-range couplers (superconducting) or atom/ion shuttling (all-to-all platforms).
  4. Decode with fast belief-propagation-style decoders, since matching works poorly for these codes.
  5. Add modules for logical gates (e.g. ancilla systems or code switching), which are harder than in surface codes.

Who uses it

IBM (whose Starling roadmap uses bivariate bicycle codes), Quantinuum, Microsoft, neutral-atom companies and QEC theorists are racing to turn high-rate codes into working hardware.

Key takeaway

Remember the trade-off in one line: surface code = simple wiring, low rate; qLDPC = high rate (many logical qubits per block), but long-range connectivity and harder logic.

Going deeper

  • IBM's bivariate bicycle codes (Bravyi et al., Nature 2024) include the [[144,12,12]] gross code; IBM's 2025 Starling architecture pairs gross and 'two-gross' [[288,12,18]] blocks with logical processing units and long-range 'c-couplers' first tested on the Loon chip (announced November 2025).
  • In 2021 Panteleev and Kalachev proved 'good' qLDPC codes exist, with constant rate and distance growing linearly in n — something impossible for 2D-local codes like the surface code (Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal bounds).
  • Colour codes allow transversal Clifford gates (H, S, CNOT); Google reported a below-threshold colour code on Willow in 2025 with Λ ≈ 1.56 from distance 3 to 5, plus logical teleportation by lattice surgery and magic-state injection.
  • Quantinuum's Helix architecture used a [[20,2,6]] code on Helios; a September 2026 preprint reported memory errors near 4.6 × 10⁻⁵ per logical qubit per cycle and logical Cliffords beating physical baselines without post-selection (not yet peer reviewed).
  • Microsoft's June 2025 '4D geometric codes' target all-to-all hardware, claiming about five-fold fewer physical qubits than surface codes and single-shot error checking; its Quantinuum collaborations used the tesseract [[16,4,4]] and carbon [[12,2,4]] codes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing codes by qubit count alone: logical-gate cost, decoder speed and connectivity requirements often dominate the real overhead.
  • Assuming qLDPC codes run on any chip: superconducting grids need new long-range couplers; ions and atoms get connectivity from movement but run slower cycles.
  • Treating every 'logical qubit' headline as equal: check the code distance, whether errors are corrected or only detected, and whether post-selection was used.

docs.title: 5.10 Bosonic Codes and Cat Qubits
docs.text:
Instead of building a logical qubit from many two-level qubits, bosonic codes store information in the many energy levels of a single microwave resonator or light mode. Cat qubits use two opposite 'coherent states' that make bit flips exponentially rare, leaving mainly phase flips — which a simple repetition code can handle. This hardware-efficient approach powers AWS's Ocelot chip and Alice & Bob's roadmap.

Ocelot-style repetition code over cat qubits. Cats store data; transmons between them measure phase-flip parities along a single line.

Think of it like…

A cat qubit is like a marble resting in one of two deep valleys far apart: shaking the table (noise) almost never pushes it over the hill to the other valley, so only the much easier-to-fix 'wobble' errors remain.

Real-world example

Sofia, an engineer at fictional Fermata Labs, studies AWS's 2025 Ocelot design: five cat qubits store data, four transmons measure phase-flip parities between neighbours, and five buffer circuits stabilise the cats. Because bit flips are suppressed in hardware, a repetition code along one line suffices, which AWS says could cut error-correction overhead by up to 90% versus conventional approaches.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Store the qubit in a resonator: |0⟩ and |1⟩ become two coherent states |α⟩ and |−α⟩ (a 'cat' pair).
  2. Continuously pump the resonator with two-photon drive and dissipation so it relaxes back into the cat manifold.
  3. Increase the average photon number |α|²: bit-flip time grows exponentially, phase-flip rate grows only linearly.
  4. Protect against the remaining phase flips with a repetition code measured by ancilla transmons.
  5. Build bias-preserving gates (e.g. CNOT that doesn't convert phase flips into bit flips) to keep the noise asymmetric.

Who uses it

AWS Center for Quantum Computing, Alice & Bob, Yale and Quantum Circuits Inc., Nord Quantique, Xanadu and other bosonic/photonic teams, plus QEC theorists working on biased noise.

Key takeaway

One-liner for interviews: cat qubits trade a 2D code for a 1D repetition code by making bit flips exponentially rare in hardware — 'hardware-efficient QEC'.

Going deeper

  • AWS announced Ocelot in February 2025 (Nature paper): five cat data qubits in tantalum-on-silicon resonators, five buffer circuits for stabilisation and four transmon ancillas measuring phase-flip syndromes — a distance-5 repetition code in about one square centimetre.
  • Alice & Bob reported in September 2025 preliminary bit-flip times beyond one hour (33-60 minutes, 95% confidence) on a 'Galvanic Cat' Helium 2 chip, up from 430 seconds in 2024; its roadmap targets about 100 logical qubits (Graphene) by 2030.
  • Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes, proposed in 2001, encode a qubit in grid-like oscillator states that correct small displacements; Yale researchers (Sivak et al., Nature 2023) showed a GKP qubit beyond breakeven, with a lifetime about 2.3 times the best physical encoding.
  • Dual-rail and erasure qubits convert the dominant error into a heralded 'erasure' whose location is known; codes tolerate erasures far better (threshold for erasures in surface codes is much higher than for unknown Pauli errors).
  • Cat-qubit overhead depends on bias-preserving gates: a CNOT between cats must not turn a phase flip into a bit flip, which is achievable because the two-photon-stabilised manifold can be rotated continuously.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking cat qubits need no error correction: phase flips actually increase with photon number, so a repetition code is still essential.
  • Comparing Ocelot to Willow by qubit count: Ocelot demonstrated a memory with hardware-suppressed bit flips, not universal logic or below-threshold scaling at large distance.
  • Assuming company roadmap numbers are measured results: Alice & Bob's and AWS's overhead savings are projections until full logical operations are shown.

docs.title: 5.11 Logical-Qubit Milestones, 2016-2026
docs.text:
Over the past decade experiments moved from protecting a single cavity qubit to dozens of logical qubits running small algorithms. Key steps were: first breakeven results, exponential error suppression in repetition codes, below-threshold surface codes (Google Willow, 2024), and large logical-qubit arrays on ions and neutral atoms (Quantinuum, Microsoft, Harvard/QuEra, Atom Computing). Headlines vary widely in what they really prove, so reading them carefully is a core skill.

From breakeven to dozens of logical qubits. Read each step for what it proves: memory, scaling, gates, or many qubits at once.

Think of it like…

It is like the history of aviation: first a hop that beat gravity for a few seconds, then controlled flight, then longer flights with passengers — each 'first' matters, but you must check whether it was a glide or a powered, steered flight.

Real-world example

Kofi, a journalist student, compares two 2025-26 headlines: '94 logical qubits' and '48 logical qubits' on the same Quantinuum Helios machine. Reading the papers, he finds the 94 were error-detected (bad runs discarded), while the 48 were error-corrected; a third experiment, Helix, beat physical baselines without discarding any runs. All three are real progress, but they measure different things.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the code and its distance: distance 2 detects, distance ≥ 3 can correct.
  2. Check whether results use post-selection (discarding flagged runs) or full real-time correction.
  3. Compare the logical error rate with the best physical qubit or gate (breakeven) and across code sizes (threshold scaling).
  4. Check what was done with the logical qubits: memory only, Clifford gates, or universal (non-Clifford) operations.
  5. Note peer-review status: many milestones first appear as preprints and change during review.

Who uses it

Analysts, investors, journalists, PhD students and hiring managers all need to read logical-qubit claims critically; QEC researchers live this timeline.

Key takeaway

Ask three questions of every logical-qubit headline: detected or corrected? post-selected or not? does error fall as the code grows?

Going deeper

  • Google's 2023 Nature paper showed a distance-5 surface code slightly outperforming distance 3 (about 2.91% vs 3.03% logical error per cycle) on Sycamore — the first time a bigger code helped; Willow then reached Λ ≈ 2.14 across distances 3-7.
  • Harvard, MIT and QuEra (Nature, December 2023) ran algorithms on up to 48 logical qubits using [[8,3,2]] colour codes on 280 atoms; these were error-detecting codes with post-selection, but they showed transversal logic on reconfigurable atom arrays.
  • Microsoft and Quantinuum reported in April 2024 four logical qubits from 30 physical qubits with logical circuit error rates up to 800× below physical; Microsoft and Atom Computing reported 24 entangled (and 28 computational) logical qubits in November 2024.
  • Quantinuum's Helios (November 2025, 98 barium ions) produced 94 error-detected logical qubits in a GHZ state and 48 error-corrected logical qubits at a 2:1 encoding ratio, with company-reported logical errors 10-100× below physical.
  • Harvard-MIT-QuEra's 2025 Nature paper used up to 448 atoms to combine surface codes, atom-loss detection, machine-learning decoding and transversal teleportation with [[15,1,3]] codes, reporting about 2.14× below-threshold performance.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Adding up logical qubits across papers as if they were equivalent: distance, post-selection and gate sets differ widely.
  • Equating 'logical qubit' with 'useful': most demonstrations are memories or small Clifford circuits; useful algorithms need non-Clifford logical gates at very low error.
  • Quoting company press releases as peer-reviewed facts: check the arXiv or journal version, which often states caveats more clearly.

docs.title: 5.12 Decoders and Real-Time Decoding
docs.text:
A decoder is the classical software or chip that reads the stream of syndrome measurements and works out which errors most likely happened. It must be accurate (to reach low logical error) and fast enough to keep up with roughly a million syndrome rounds per second on superconducting hardware. Decoders range from classic graph algorithms (matching, union-find) to belief propagation and neural networks such as Google DeepMind's AlphaQubit.

The real-time decoding loop. The decoder must keep pace with every round and answer quickly when a logical decision is needed.

Think of it like…

A decoder is like an air-traffic controller watching radar blips: each blip (detection event) is ambiguous on its own, but by pairing them up across space and time the controller reconstructs which planes went where — and must do it in real time.

Real-world example

Corvid Quantum (fictional) runs a distance-11 memory with a 1 µs cycle. Its software MWPM decoder averages 3 µs per round, so a backlog grows each round and the computation would stall. Switching to an FPGA union-find decoder at 0.6 µs per round keeps up, at a small accuracy cost; the team then tests a neural decoder offline to see how much accuracy it could win back.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Convert raw stabiliser measurements into detection events (changes between rounds).
  2. Build a model of which faults trigger which detectors (a detector error model or decoding graph).
  3. Find the most likely set of faults consistent with the observed detection events (matching, union-find, BP or a neural network).
  4. Output a correction or update the Pauli frame, especially before any non-Clifford gate that needs the answer.
  5. Keep throughput above the syndrome rate; otherwise a backlog builds and computation slows exponentially.

Who uses it

QEC software engineers, FPGA/ASIC designers (Riverlane, IBM, Google), machine-learning researchers (Google DeepMind) and control-system teams build and deploy decoders.

Key takeaway

Separate the two speed metrics: throughput (must match the cycle rate, e.g. ~1 µs) and latency (time to answer when a feed-forward decision is needed, ideally ~10 µs or less).

Going deeper

  • Minimum-weight perfect matching (Dennis et al., 2002, using Edmonds' blossom algorithm) pairs detection events in a graph; PyMatching 2's 'sparse blossom' (Higgott & Gidney) decodes about a million errors per core-second for surface codes.
  • Union-find decoding (Delfosse & Nickerson) grows clusters around detection events in almost-linear time, giving slightly lower accuracy than matching but suiting FPGA and ASIC implementation.
  • qLDPC codes break matching's assumptions, so IBM developed Relay-BP (2025), a belief-propagation variant; an IBM FPGA prototype reported 24 ns per BP iteration and sub-microsecond average decoding per cycle for the gross code.
  • AlphaQubit (Google DeepMind & Quantum AI, Nature 2024) used a transformer-based neural network to beat matching accuracy on Sycamore data; an AlphaQubit 2 preprint (December 2025) reports real-time variants under 1 µs per cycle up to distance 11.
  • If average decoding time exceeds the cycle time, unprocessed syndrome data accumulates (the 'backlog problem', Terhal 2015), so throughput, not just accuracy, sets hardware requirements; sliding-window and parallel decoders split the work.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Benchmarking decoders only on accuracy: a decoder too slow for the cycle rate is unusable in a real machine, however accurate.
  • Assuming every gate needs an immediate correction: Clifford gates can rely on Pauli-frame tracking; only non-Clifford steps need low-latency answers.
  • Using matching for every code: it is near-optimal for surface codes but performs poorly on colour and qLDPC codes without extensions.

docs.title: Try it: Simulate a distance-3 surface-code memory and decode it with matching (pip install stim pymatching)
docs.text:
import stim, pymatching

circuit = stim.Circuit.generated(
    "surface_code:rotated_memory_z", distance=3, rounds=3,
    after_clifford_depolarization=0.001)
sampler = circuit.compile_detector_sampler()
dets, obs = sampler.sample(shots=100_000, separate_observables=True)

dem = circuit.detector_error_model(decompose_errors=True)
matching = pymatching.Matching.from_detector_error_model(dem)
pred = matching.decode_batch(dets)
errors = (pred != obs).any(axis=1).sum()
print(f"logical error rate: {errors / 100_000:.5f}")

docs.title: 5.13 Magic States: Distillation and Cultivation
docs.text:
Error-correcting codes make some gates (the Clifford gates) easy and safe, but no code can make every gate easy — and Clifford gates alone can't beat classical computers. The missing ingredient, usually the T gate, is supplied by preparing special 'magic states', purifying them, and teleporting them into the circuit. Producing these states cheaply is one of the biggest costs of a fault-tolerant computer.

From noisy state to logical T gate. Distillation multiplies quality at the cost of many input states; cultivation aims to do it with far fewer qubits.

Think of it like…

It is like a bakery whose ovens can make any bread except one ingredient — yeast — which must be cultured separately, filtered for purity, and then mixed in exactly when needed.

Real-world example

Helix Analytics' (fictional) chemistry algorithm needs 10⁹ T gates. Raw injected magic states have about 10⁻³ error. One round of 15-to-1 distillation turns 15 such states into one with error about 35 × (10⁻³)³ ≈ 3.5 × 10⁻⁸ — not enough for 10⁹ gates — so the team plans two rounds or 'magic state cultivation', which Google researchers proposed in 2024 as a much cheaper route.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Inject: prepare a noisy magic state |T⟩ = T|+⟩ on a physical qubit and encode it into a small code patch.
  2. Purify: distil many noisy copies into fewer, better ones (e.g. 15-to-1), or 'cultivate' a single state by repeated checks with post-selection.
  3. Store the purified state until needed in a factory output buffer.
  4. Teleport: consume the state with a CNOT and measurement to apply a logical T gate to a data qubit.
  5. Fix up: half the time the measurement requires a Clifford correction (S gate), applied or tracked in software.

Who uses it

Fault-tolerant architects, resource-estimation teams and QEC experimentalists; magic-state factories often dominate qubit counts in algorithm cost estimates.

Key takeaway

Know the chain of reasoning: Eastin-Knill says no code has a transversal universal gate set → Clifford + T is universal → T via magic states → cost dominated by factories.

Going deeper

  • The Eastin-Knill theorem (2009) proves no quantum code can implement a universal gate set transversally, so every fault-tolerant scheme needs an extra trick such as magic states, code switching or gauge fixing.
  • Bravyi and Kitaev's 2005 15-to-1 protocol uses the [[15,1,3]] Reed-Muller code: 15 noisy T states yield one with error about 35p³ when it passes the checks; Litinski (2019) showed optimised factories are far cheaper than early estimates.
  • Magic state cultivation (Gidney, Shutty & Jones, 2024) grows a T state inside a small colour code with repeated checks and post-selection, then expands it into a surface code, reaching about 10⁻⁹ error with a footprint similar to a single logical qubit.
  • A Google-led December 2025 preprint demonstrated cultivation on superconducting hardware, reporting a 40-fold error reduction and state fidelity of about 0.9999 while keeping 8% of attempts; Quantinuum (2025) reported logical magic states beating physical error in a [[6,2,2]] code.
  • Algorithms are costed by their T-count or Toffoli count; synthesising an arbitrary rotation to precision ε needs about 3·log₂(1/ε) T gates using optimal methods such as gridsynth (Ross & Selinger), now Qiskit's default RZ synthesis in discrete bases since version 2.4.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking T gates are 'just another gate': in fault-tolerant machines they can cost 100-1,000 times more space-time than Clifford gates.
  • Ignoring post-selection rates: cultivation and distillation discard failed attempts, so throughput (states per second) matters as much as fidelity.
  • Assuming one round of distillation is always enough: target error depends on the algorithm's total T-count, often needing two rounds or cultivation plus distillation.

docs.title: 5.14 Fault-Tolerant Resource Estimates and the Road to FTQC
docs.text:
Resource estimates translate an algorithm into the physical machine needed to run it: how many physical qubits, how long, at what error rates. They show that useful fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs hundreds to thousands of logical qubits and millions to billions of reliable operations. Vendors now publish roadmaps aimed at exactly these targets, with IBM, Quantinuum, Google, Microsoft and others aiming for the late 2020s to early 2030s.

Announced steps toward fault tolerance (plans, not guarantees). Dates are company targets as of October 2026; treat later ones with growing scepticism.

Think of it like…

A resource estimate is like an architect's bill of materials for a skyscraper: before pouring concrete you know how many beams, workers and months you need — and roadmaps are the developer's promised completion dates, which may slip.

Real-world example

Ravi, an analyst at fictional Meridian Bank, reads that breaking RSA-2048 was estimated at 20 million noisy qubits in 2019 but under one million in Gidney's 2025 paper (under a week of runtime), and that a 2026 preprint claims under 100,000 using qLDPC codes. He notes all assume 0.1% gate errors and 1 µs cycles on machines that don't yet exist, and he presents both the trend and the caveats to his security team.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write the algorithm as logical operations and count logical qubits plus T/Toffoli gates.
  2. Choose a code, target logical error per operation and therefore a code distance.
  3. Add factory, routing and storage space to get total physical qubits.
  4. Multiply operation counts by code-cycle and reaction times to get runtime.
  5. Compare the required machine with vendor roadmaps, discounting for schedule risk.

Who uses it

Quantum architects, security teams planning post-quantum migration, investors, government programmes and vendor strategy groups all read these estimates and roadmaps.

Key takeaway

Remember IBM's targets: Starling (2029) with 200 logical qubits running 100 million operations, then Blue Jay (2033 or later) with about 2,000 logical qubits and a billion operations.

Going deeper

  • Gidney's May 2025 RSA-2048 estimate (under one million noisy qubits, under a week) assumes a square grid, 0.1% gate error, 1 µs surface-code cycle and 10 µs reaction time; the savings come from approximate arithmetic, yoked surface codes and magic state cultivation.
  • In 2026 two preprints lowered estimates further: Iceberg Quantum's 'Pinnacle' qLDPC architecture claimed RSA-2048 with under 100,000 physical qubits (February), and a Google-led paper estimated 256-bit elliptic-curve keys with under 500,000 qubits (March) — both theoretical.
  • Preskill's 'megaquop' framing (2024) sets a near-term goal of about a million reliable logical operations — beyond what error mitigation can reach — before 'gigaquop' and 'teraquop' machines for chemistry and cryptanalysis.
  • Google's six-milestone roadmap runs from beyond-classical (2019) and a QEC prototype (2023) to a long-lived logical qubit (one error per million operations), a logical gate, about 100 logical qubits, and finally a million-physical-qubit error-corrected computer.
  • Space-time volume (qubits × cycles) is the fairest single cost metric because designs trade qubits for time; a faster but bigger machine and a slower but smaller one can have similar volume.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading a roadmap date as a delivery date: quantum roadmaps have slipped before, and later milestones depend on unsolved engineering problems.
  • Comparing resource estimates with different assumptions: error rates, cycle times, connectivity and code choice can change answers by 10× or more.
  • Concluding RSA is safe because no machine exists yet: data harvested today can be decrypted later, so migration planning must start long before the hardware arrives.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Programming Quantum Computers
docs.text: Quantum programs are hybrid: classical code builds, compiles and analyses circuits that run on a quantum processor or simulator. This chapter walks through the main toolkits — Qiskit 2.x and IBM's runtime, Cirq, PennyLane, CUDA-Q, Q# and Azure Quantum, Amazon Braket, pytket and Guppy — plus interchange formats, simulators, cloud pricing, your first working circuits, and the testing and engineering habits that make quantum code reliable. Code snippets use APIs current as of October 2026.

docs.title: 6.1 The Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflow
docs.text:
Real quantum programs are mostly classical code. A normal computer prepares the problem, builds and compiles circuits, sends them to a quantum processor (QPU) for many repeated 'shots', and then analyses the results — often in a loop where a classical optimiser adjusts circuit parameters and tries again. Learning to program quantum computers means learning this whole pipeline, not just the gates.

The hybrid loop. The QPU is one step in a classical loop; latency between steps often dominates total runtime.

Think of it like…

It is like a chef (the classical computer) who tastes a sauce, adjusts the seasoning and sends it back to a special oven (the QPU) that only it can operate — round after round until the dish is right.

Real-world example

Aisha, a data scientist at fictional GreenGrid Energy, estimates the ground-state energy of a toy two-qubit Hamiltonian. Her Python script builds a parameterised circuit, asks an Estimator for the energy, and lets SciPy's COBYLA optimiser change the angles. After a few dozen rounds the energy reaches −1.4142, matching the exact answer computed by diagonalising the 4 × 4 matrix.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Map: translate the business or science problem into qubits, circuits and observables (e.g. a Hamiltonian).
  2. Optimise: transpile circuits for the target hardware's native gates and connectivity.
  3. Execute: run batches of circuits on a simulator or QPU through primitives such as Sampler and Estimator.
  4. Post-process: apply error mitigation, compute statistics and feed the result to a classical optimiser or analysis step.
  5. Repeat the loop until the answer converges, logging job IDs and settings for reproducibility.

Who uses it

Quantum software engineers, application scientists in chemistry, finance and logistics, and HPC teams integrating QPUs with supercomputers all build hybrid workflows.

Key takeaway

IBM calls this pipeline 'Qiskit patterns': Map → Optimise → Execute → Post-process — a handy structure for interview answers and project write-ups.

Going deeper

  • Each QPU execution returns samples, not amplitudes: estimating an expectation value to precision ε needs on the order of 1/ε² shots, so 1% precision costs about 10,000 shots per observable group.
  • Queueing and network latency can exceed QPU time by orders of magnitude; execution modes such as IBM sessions and batches, or Braket Hybrid Jobs, keep the classical loop close to the QPU and give priority access.
  • Primitives separate what you want (samples from Sampler, expectation values from Estimator) from how the provider gets it, letting vendors add error suppression and mitigation server- or client-side without changing your code.
  • IBM's 'quantum-centric supercomputing' vision and work such as sample-based quantum diagonalisation (SQD) run large classical post-processing on HPC nodes, using the QPU to propose important configurations.
  • HPC centres integrate QPUs with job schedulers such as Slurm and with GPU clusters; NVIDIA's NVQLink and CUDA-Q target low-latency coupling for workloads like real-time decoding.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the QPU runs your whole program: it executes only the circuit; loops, optimisers and data handling stay classical.
  • Ignoring shot noise: an optimiser chasing random fluctuations can wander; choose noise-robust optimisers such as SPSA or COBYLA and enough shots.
  • Submitting each iteration as a separate queued job on a busy device: use sessions, batching or hybrid-job services to avoid hours of waiting.

docs.title: Try it: A tiny variational loop: classical optimiser + quantum Estimator (pip install qiskit scipy)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from qiskit.circuit.library import real_amplitudes
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorEstimator

H = SparsePauliOp(["ZZ", "XI", "IX"], coeffs=[1.0, 0.5, 0.5])  # toy Hamiltonian
ansatz = real_amplitudes(2, reps=2)
est = StatevectorEstimator()

def energy(x):                       # quantum side: estimate <H>
    return float(est.run([(ansatz, H, x)]).result()[0].data.evs)

res = minimize(energy, np.zeros(ansatz.num_parameters), method="COBYLA")
print("VQE energy:", round(res.fun, 4))                       # -1.4142
print("exact     :", round(min(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H.to_matrix())), 4))

docs.title: 6.2 Qiskit SDK 2.x: Circuits, Transpiler and Primitives
docs.text:
Qiskit is IBM's open-source Python toolkit and the most widely used quantum SDK. You build circuits with QuantumCircuit, analyse states and operators with quantum_info, compile ('transpile') circuits for real hardware, and run them through the Sampler and Estimator primitives. The 2.x series (2.0 in 2025; 2.5.2 in August 2026) moved performance-critical code to Rust and added a C API.

The Qiskit SDK stack. Your code sits on top; the same primitives interface reaches simulators or real QPUs.

Think of it like…

Qiskit is like a full workshop for a new kind of furniture: a design bench (circuits), measuring tools (quantum_info), a machine that cuts designs to fit a specific room (transpiler), and a delivery service (primitives) to whichever house — simulator or QPU — you choose.

Real-world example

Tomás, a computer-science undergraduate, writes a Bell-state circuit, checks its expectation value ⟨ZZ⟩ = 2 for the observable ZZ + XX + ZI with StatevectorEstimator, then transpiles it for a simulated backend at optimisation level 1. The compiled circuit has depth 3 with one CX; Aer's sampler returns about half '00' and half '11'.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. pip install qiskit (plus qiskit-aer for fast noisy simulation).
  2. Build a QuantumCircuit, or use the circuit library (QFT, real_amplitudes, etc.).
  3. Inspect it with quantum_info (Statevector, Operator, SparsePauliOp) and draw it.
  4. Transpile with generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level, backend) to get an ISA circuit.
  5. Run PUBs (circuit, observables, parameter values) through Sampler or Estimator and read results from DataBin fields.

Who uses it

Students, researchers and professional quantum developers worldwide; Qiskit skills appear in most quantum software job adverts and IBM's developer certification.

Key takeaway

Know the V2 primitive result shape: result[0].data.meas.get_counts() for Sampler (register 'meas' from measure_all) and result[0].data.evs for Estimator.

Going deeper

  • Qiskit follows semantic versioning with a new minor release about every three months; 2.0 (March 2025) removed qiskit.pulse, the V1 primitives and BackendV1, and later 2.x releases stayed backwards-compatible within the series.
  • Qiskit 2.4 made gridsynth the default for synthesising RZ rotations into Clifford+T and allowed Python extensions built on the C API; 2.5 added a MultiStagePassManager and Clifford+T and Pauli-based-computation presets, with typical 2-3× faster transpilation on Benchpress circuits.
  • A PUB (primitive unified bloc) bundles one circuit with observables and parameter values; Estimator broadcasts arrays of parameters and observables, so one job can evaluate many points of a parameter sweep.
  • Transpilation runs stages init → layout → routing → translation → optimisation → scheduling; Sabre layout and routing insert SWAPs for limited connectivity, and optimisation_level 0-3 trades compile time for fewer gates.
  • ISA (instruction set architecture) circuits use only the backend's native gates and connectivity; IBM hardware rejects non-ISA circuits, so always transpile first and call observable.apply_layout(isa.layout) for Estimator jobs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Following pre-2024 tutorials: execute(), Aer.get_backend(), BackendV1 and V1 primitives are gone in Qiskit 2.x; use primitives and pass managers.
  • Forgetting Qiskit's little-endian bit order: qubit 0 is the rightmost character in result bitstrings.
  • Sending untranspiled circuits or forgetting apply_layout on observables, which gives errors or silently wrong qubit mappings.

docs.title: Try it: Qiskit 2.x basics: local primitives and transpilation (pip install qiskit qiskit-aer)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorSampler, StatevectorEstimator
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from qiskit.transpiler import generate_preset_pass_manager
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

bell = QuantumCircuit(2); bell.h(0); bell.cx(0, 1)

# Estimator: expectation values
obs = SparsePauliOp(["ZZ", "XX", "ZI"])
print(StatevectorEstimator().run([(bell, obs)]).result()[0].data.evs)   # 2.0

# Sampler: bitstrings
meas = bell.measure_all(inplace=False)
res = StatevectorSampler().run([meas], shots=1000).result()
print(res[0].data.meas.get_counts())                                  # ~{'00': 500, '11': 500}

# Transpile to a backend's instruction set (ISA)
pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level=1, backend=AerSimulator())
isa = pm.run(meas)
print(isa.count_ops(), isa.depth())

docs.title: 6.3 IBM Quantum Platform, Runtime Primitives and Qiskit Functions
docs.text:
IBM Quantum Platform is IBM's cloud service for running Qiskit programs on real IBM QPUs. You authenticate with an API key, pick a backend, transpile, and submit jobs through Sampler and Estimator, which can apply error suppression and mitigation for you. In 2026 IBM renamed the service 'IBM Quantum Compute service' (formerly Qiskit Runtime) and moved its primitives to a new client-side design built on an 'Executor'.

Submitting a job to IBM Quantum Platform. Compile locally, execute remotely; usage is billed in QPU time, not wall-clock queue time.

Think of it like…

It is like a professional print shop: you upload a press-ready file (an ISA circuit), choose quality options (error mitigation), and the shop schedules it on its presses and sends back the prints with a bill measured in minutes of press time.

Real-world example

Chen, a researcher at fictional Lakeside University, uses her Open Plan account (10 free QPU minutes per 28 days). She saves her API key once, asks for the least-busy 100+ qubit device, transpiles a 20-qubit GHZ circuit and runs 4,000 shots with Sampler. The job uses a few seconds of QPU time, so she can run many experiments before her allowance runs out.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Create an IBM Cloud account and Quantum instance; copy the API key and instance CRN.
  2. Save credentials once with QiskitRuntimeService.save_account(...) — keep keys out of notebooks and Git.
  3. Choose a backend (service.least_busy(...)) and transpile circuits to ISA form for it.
  4. Pick a primitive and options (shots, resilience level, dynamical decoupling, twirling) and an execution mode (job, batch or session).
  5. Submit, record the job ID, and retrieve results and usage later from the dashboard or API.

Who uses it

Researchers, students and enterprise teams using IBM hardware; IBM Quantum Network members such as universities, banks and labs run most of their experiments this way.

Key takeaway

As of qiskit-ibm-runtime 0.50 (September 2026), import Sampler and Estimator from executor_sampler / executor_estimator; the old server-side SamplerV2/EstimatorV2 classes are deprecated but follow the same interface.

Going deeper

  • qiskit-ibm-runtime 0.47 (May 2026) introduced the Executor primitive and QuantumProgram, built with the samplomatic package for circuit annotations and randomisation; the directed execution model is labelled beta, and IBM says new capabilities will arrive in Executor first.
  • Release 0.49 (August 2026) renamed Qiskit Runtime to IBM Quantum Compute service (QiskitRuntimeService is also available as IBMQuantumComputeService); 0.50 (September 2026) added client-side Sampler and Estimator that pre- and post-process locally and run through Executor.
  • Execution modes: job (single request), batch (many independent jobs scheduled together) and session (exclusive iterative access); sessions are not available on the free Open Plan.
  • Qiskit Functions are higher-level services from IBM and partners — e.g. Q-CTRL's Fire Opal, Kipu Quantum's Iskay optimiser, Qunova's HI-VQE chemistry — available to Premium, Flex and On-Prem plan users, some as free trials.
  • Qiskit addons are open-source research tools that run alongside the primitives: SQD (sample-based quantum diagonalisation), OBP (operator backpropagation), MPF (multi-product formulas), circuit cutting and AQC-Tensor.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pasting your API key into a notebook you later share: save it with save_account or an environment variable and rotate it if exposed.
  • Copying older tutorials that use the retired 'ibm_quantum' channel or execute(): update to current QiskitRuntimeService and primitive imports.
  • Forgetting that mitigation multiplies QPU time: higher resilience levels or many twirls consume your minutes faster.

docs.title: Try it: Run a Bell circuit on IBM hardware (pip install qiskit "qiskit-ibm-runtime>=0.50"; uses QPU time)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.transpiler import generate_preset_pass_manager
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
from qiskit_ibm_runtime.executor_sampler import Sampler
# older clients (< 0.50): from qiskit_ibm_runtime import SamplerV2 as Sampler

# one-time setup, stores credentials locally:
# QiskitRuntimeService.save_account(token="<your API key>", instance="<your CRN>")
service = QiskitRuntimeService()
backend = service.least_busy(operational=True, simulator=False)

qc = QuantumCircuit(2); qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure_all()
isa = generate_preset_pass_manager(backend=backend, optimization_level=1).run(qc)

job = Sampler(mode=backend).run([isa], shots=1000)
print("job id:", job.job_id())
print(job.result()[0].data.meas.get_counts())

docs.title: 6.4 Cirq and Google's Quantum Software
docs.text:
Cirq is Google Quantum AI's open-source Python framework for writing and running quantum circuits, designed around the details of real hardware such as qubit grids and timing 'moments'. Around it sit fast simulators (qsim), the Stim error-correction simulator, OpenFermion for chemistry and Qualtran for fault-tolerant algorithm design. Google's own Willow processors are accessed by selected research partners rather than a public cloud.

The Cirq ecosystem. Cirq is the hub; specialised tools cover simulation, error correction, chemistry and fault-tolerant design.

Think of it like…

If Qiskit is a well-stocked general workshop, Cirq is a precision lab bench built by the team that designs the instruments — very close to how the hardware actually behaves.

Real-world example

Ingrid, a physics master's student, writes a Bell circuit in Cirq with two LineQubits, simulates 1,000 repetitions and gets about 500 each of 0 and 3 (binary 00 and 11) in the histogram. She then swaps to qsim to simulate a 30-qubit random circuit on her workstation and uses Stim for a surface-code study in her QEC course.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. pip install cirq (or cirq-core plus vendor modules such as cirq-google or cirq-ionq).
  2. Create qubits (LineQubit, GridQubit) and build a Circuit from operations organised into Moments.
  3. Simulate with cirq.Simulator, or qsimcirq for larger circuits.
  4. Apply transformers to optimise or compile circuits for a target device's gate set.
  5. Run on hardware through a vendor service (e.g. IonQ, Azure Quantum) or Google's access programmes.

Who uses it

Google Quantum AI researchers and partners, QEC researchers (Stim, PyMatching), chemistry teams using OpenFermion, and developers targeting IonQ, AQT or Pasqal through Cirq modules.

Key takeaway

Cirq results come back as integer-keyed histograms per measurement key; know that measurement keys, not classical registers, organise Cirq results.

Going deeper

  • Cirq organises circuits into Moments — sets of operations that happen at the same time on disjoint qubits — which makes timing and hardware scheduling explicit; cirq 1.7 was current on PyPI in October 2026.
  • qsim is a C++ state-vector simulator with a Cirq interface (qsimcirq); Google states it can simulate up to about 40 qubits on a 90-core Intel Xeon workstation, and it supports GPU acceleration via cuQuantum.
  • Stim, written by Craig Gidney, simulates stabiliser circuits extremely fast and generates detector error models; with PyMatching it is the standard open toolchain for surface-code research.
  • Google opened a Willow Early Access Program in 2026 for selected research teams, with proposals due 15 May 2026; Google does not offer general public cloud access to its processors.
  • Qualtran expresses fault-tolerant algorithms as composable 'bloqs' and counts logical resources such as T and Toffoli gates, while OpenFermion converts molecular problems into qubit Hamiltonians.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting Cirq to give you Google hardware access: you still need a programme invitation or a third-party provider.
  • Mixing up Cirq's integer histograms with bitstring orders: measurement key order determines which qubit is the most significant bit.
  • Using Cirq's default simulator for large circuits: switch to qsim or a GPU backend above roughly 20-25 qubits.

docs.title: Try it: Bell state in Cirq (pip install cirq)
docs.text:
import cirq

q0, q1 = cirq.LineQubit.range(2)
circuit = cirq.Circuit(
    cirq.H(q0),
    cirq.CNOT(q0, q1),
    cirq.measure(q0, q1, key="m"),
)
print(circuit)
result = cirq.Simulator().run(circuit, repetitions=1000)
print(result.histogram(key="m"))   # Counter({0: ~500, 3: ~500}) -> 00 and 11

docs.title: 6.5 PennyLane and Differentiable Quantum Programming
docs.text:
PennyLane, created by Xanadu, treats quantum circuits like functions you can differentiate, just as deep-learning libraries do with neural networks. You write a Python function, decorate it as a QNode attached to a device, and PennyLane computes gradients automatically — on simulators or real hardware via plugins. It is the most popular framework for quantum machine learning and variational algorithms.

Training a circuit in PennyLane. The same loop as training a neural network — the circuit is just another differentiable layer.

Think of it like…

PennyLane is like adding an automatic slope gauge to a hiking map: wherever you stand on the landscape of circuit parameters, it tells you which way is downhill so an optimiser can walk to the valley.

Real-world example

Lucas, an ML engineer at fictional Orbit Analytics, defines a two-qubit QNode returning ⟨Z⟩ on the second qubit after RY(θ) and CNOT. PennyLane reports the value cos(0.3) ≈ 0.955 and gradient −sin(0.3) ≈ −0.296; sixty gradient-descent steps drive the value to −1.0 at θ = π. He then swaps the device string to a GPU simulator without changing the circuit code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. pip install pennylane (plus a plugin or lightning.gpu for other backends).
  2. Create a device: qml.device('default.qubit', wires=2) or a hardware plugin device.
  3. Write the circuit as a Python function and decorate it with @qml.qnode(dev).
  4. Return measurements such as qml.expval, qml.probs or qml.sample.
  5. Differentiate with qml.grad or a JAX/PyTorch interface and optimise; optionally compile with qml.qjit (Catalyst).

Who uses it

Quantum machine-learning researchers, variational-algorithm developers, chemistry teams and educators; PennyLane's demos and Codebook are common learning resources.

Key takeaway

Remember the parameter-shift rule: for rotation gates, the exact gradient equals half the difference of the circuit evaluated at θ + π/2 and θ − π/2 — it works on real hardware.

Going deeper

  • PennyLane 0.45 was current in October 2026; its differentiation methods include backpropagation (fast on simulators), adjoint differentiation (memory-efficient for state-vector simulators) and parameter-shift (works on hardware, costing two circuit runs per parameter).
  • The Lightning simulators (lightning.qubit for CPUs, lightning.gpu via NVIDIA cuQuantum, lightning.kokkos for many architectures) are C++ back ends that speed up gradients for tens of qubits.
  • Catalyst compiles hybrid programs with qml.qjit using MLIR and LLVM, so classical control flow and quantum operations run as one compiled program rather than many Python calls.
  • Plugins connect PennyLane to Qiskit/IBM, Amazon Braket, Cirq, Quantinuum and other back ends; Braket Hybrid Jobs can run PennyLane's embedded simulators with no extra per-minute simulator charge.
  • PennyLane Datasets provide pre-computed molecular Hamiltonians and spin systems, and the Codebook offers structured interactive lessons used by many beginners.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using parameter-shift on a simulator with thousands of parameters: backprop or adjoint differentiation is far faster there.
  • Importing NumPy instead of pennylane.numpy (with autograd) and wondering why gradients are zero or missing.
  • Assuming quantum ML beats classical ML by default: barren plateaus and dequantisation results mean benchmarks against strong classical baselines are essential.

docs.title: Try it: A differentiable QNode and gradient descent (pip install pennylane)
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
from pennylane import numpy as np

dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=2)

@qml.qnode(dev)
def circuit(theta):
    qml.RY(theta, wires=0)
    qml.CNOT(wires=[0, 1])
    return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(1))          # = cos(theta)

theta = np.array(0.3, requires_grad=True)
print(circuit(theta), qml.grad(circuit)(theta))   # 0.955, -0.296

opt = qml.GradientDescentOptimizer(stepsize=0.4)
for _ in range(60):
    theta = opt.step(circuit, theta)
print("minimum:", round(float(circuit(theta)), 4))  # -1.0

docs.title: 6.6 NVIDIA CUDA-Q and GPU-Accelerated Quantum Development
docs.text:
CUDA-Q is NVIDIA's open-source platform for writing quantum 'kernels' in Python or C++ that run on GPU-accelerated simulators or real QPUs from several vendors. It is designed for hybrid workloads where GPUs and QPUs work side by side — simulation, optimisation and increasingly real-time error-correction decoding. NVIDIA also links QPUs and GPUs with low-latency hardware (NVQLink).

How a CUDA-Q kernel reaches hardware. One kernel, many targets: the compiler lowers it once and the target decides where it runs.

Think of it like…

CUDA-Q is like a universal power adapter plus a turbo generator: one plug fits many quantum devices, and when no device is attached, the GPU 'generator' simulates them very quickly.

Real-world example

Sanjay, an HPC engineer at fictional Polar Labs, writes a Bell kernel with @cudaq.kernel and samples it on his laptop CPU. On the lab's A100 node he adds cudaq.set_target('nvidia') and simulates a 32-qubit version in seconds, then switches the target string to a cloud QPU provider for a hardware run — the kernel code stays the same.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. pip install cudaq (Linux and, since 0.14, macOS CPU support; GPU targets need NVIDIA GPUs).
  2. Write a kernel with @cudaq.kernel using qvector, gates and mz measurements.
  3. Choose a target with cudaq.set_target: qpp-cpu, nvidia (GPU state vector), tensornet, or a QPU provider.
  4. Call cudaq.sample for counts or cudaq.observe for expectation values of spin operators.
  5. Scale up with multi-GPU or multi-QPU targets, or add libraries such as CUDA-Q QEC and Solvers.

Who uses it

HPC centres, GPU-heavy research groups, quantum hardware companies integrating with NVIDIA systems, and developers needing very fast simulation for algorithm research.

Key takeaway

Remember that CUDA-Q kernels are compiled (via MLIR to QIR), not interpreted Python — so only the supported subset of Python works inside a kernel.

Going deeper

  • CUDA-Q's compiler lowers kernels through MLIR dialects such as Quake to QIR and LLVM, so the same kernel can target simulators or hardware; cudaq 0.16 was the latest PyPI release in October 2026.
  • GPU targets build on NVIDIA's cuQuantum libraries: 'nvidia' uses cuStateVec for state vectors (single or multi-GPU), while 'tensornet' and 'tensornet-mps' use cuTensorNet for larger, less entangled circuits.
  • CUDA-Q 0.14 (GTC 2026) added macOS CPU support, a Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batch Execution feature for noisy simulation, and a first release of CUDA-Q Realtime for low-latency FPGA-GPU data transfer over NVQLink.
  • CUDA-Q QEC provides decoders and QEC experiment tools that run on GPUs, and CUDA-Q Solvers packages algorithms such as VQE and ADAPT-VQE for chemistry workloads.
  • NVQLink, announced by NVIDIA in 2025, is an open architecture for connecting QPU control systems to GPU supercomputers with microsecond-scale latency, aimed at real-time decoding and calibration.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing arbitrary Python inside a kernel: only a supported subset compiles, so keep data processing outside the kernel.
  • Assuming GPUs remove exponential cost: a 40-qubit state vector still needs 16 TiB in double precision; GPUs only make the feasible range faster.
  • Choosing the state-vector target for wide, shallow circuits: tensor-network targets often handle 50-plus qubits when entanglement is limited.

docs.title: Try it: A CUDA-Q kernel (pip install cudaq; GPU optional)
docs.text:
import cudaq

@cudaq.kernel
def bell():
    q = cudaq.qvector(2)
    h(q[0])
    x.ctrl(q[0], q[1])      # CNOT
    mz(q)

# cudaq.set_target("nvidia")   # uncomment on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU
print(cudaq.draw(bell))
print(cudaq.sample(bell, shots_count=1000))   # e.g. { 00:503 11:497 }

docs.title: 6.7 Q#, the Microsoft QDK and Azure Quantum
docs.text:
Q# is Microsoft's programming language designed specifically for quantum algorithms, with types like Qubit and Result and automatic qubit management. The Microsoft Quantum Development Kit (QDK) bundles Q#, a VS Code extension, simulators and a resource estimator, and its Python package can also compile OpenQASM, Qiskit, Cirq and PennyLane programs. Azure Quantum is the cloud service that sends jobs to partner hardware from IonQ, Quantinuum, Pasqal and Rigetti.

From Q# to partner hardware. The QDK compiles many front ends to QIR; Azure Quantum routes it to a provider's target.

Think of it like…

Q# is like a language invented for writing sheet music for one instrument: everything in it — notes, rests, tempo — is designed around that instrument, while Azure Quantum is the concert hall booking system for several orchestras.

Real-world example

Grace, a .NET developer at fictional Harbour Insurance, installs the QDK extension in VS Code, writes a Q# Bell operation and runs it on the built-in simulator: ten shots return pairs of matching Results such as (Zero, Zero) and (One, One). She then uses qsharp.run from Python in a notebook, and finally submits the same program to an Azure Quantum simulator target from her workspace.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Install the QDK extension for VS Code (or use vscode.dev/quantum in a browser), and pip install "qdk[azure,jupyter]" for Python.
  2. Write Q# operations: allocate qubits with use, apply gates, measure with M or MResetZ.
  3. Run and debug locally on the built-in sparse simulator, viewing circuit diagrams and histograms.
  4. Estimate fault-tolerant resources for larger algorithms with the built-in resource estimator.
  5. Create an Azure Quantum workspace, choose a provider target and QIR profile, then submit jobs and fetch results.

Who uses it

Developers in the Microsoft ecosystem, researchers estimating fault-tolerant resources, and organisations using Azure for cloud access to multiple hardware vendors.

Key takeaway

Know the target profiles: Base (no mid-circuit feedback) versus Adaptive (limited classical control after measurement) — your program must fit the profile the hardware supports.

Going deeper

  • The modern QDK (1.0 released in early 2024) was rewritten in Rust for speed and runs in browsers via WebAssembly; the qdk Python package (1.33 in October 2026) now bundles Q#, OpenQASM compilation, Azure submission and framework adapters.
  • Q# separates operations (which act on qubits) from functions (pure classical logic), manages qubit allocation with use blocks, and requires qubits to be reset before release; the standard library lives in Std.* namespaces.
  • Azure Quantum's provider list in 2026 includes IonQ (Aria, Forte), Quantinuum (H2 machines and emulators), Pasqal (Fresnel neutral atoms) and Rigetti (Cepheus-1-108Q), with Quantum Circuits Inc. listed as coming soon.
  • Jobs are compiled to QIR under a target profile (Base or Adaptive); from 11 January 2027 Azure Quantum will require new workspace data-access roles to view results or submit jobs.
  • The QDK's resource estimator models different qubit technologies and QEC schemes to report physical qubits and runtime for fault-tolerant programs, complementing Microsoft's work on 4D codes and the Magne machine.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting Q# code using arbitrary mid-circuit branching to run on every target: Base-profile hardware rejects it; check the target profile first.
  • Forgetting to reset qubits before they go out of scope: Q# expects released qubits to be back in |0⟩, so use MResetZ or Reset.
  • Following tutorials for the pre-2024 'classic' QDK (.NET-based IQ# kernel): syntax and tooling changed significantly.

docs.title: Try it: Q# Bell pair from Python (pip install "qdk[jupyter]")
docs.text:
from qdk import qsharp

qsharp.eval("""
operation Bell() : (Result, Result) {
    use (a, b) = (Qubit(), Qubit());
    H(a);
    CNOT(a, b);
    return (MResetZ(a), MResetZ(b));
}
""")
print(qsharp.run("Bell()", shots=10))   # e.g. [(Zero, Zero), (One, One), ...]

docs.title: 6.8 Amazon Braket and its SDK
docs.text:
Amazon Braket is AWS's managed quantum service, giving pay-as-you-go access to hardware from several companies — trapped ions, superconducting chips and neutral atoms — plus managed simulators. The open-source Braket Python SDK lets you build circuits, test them free on a local simulator, then send the same code to a QPU. Billing is per task plus per shot, so costs are easy to predict.

Cost of one 1,000-shot task on Braket QPUs. $0.30 per task plus per-shot fees (AWS list prices, October 2026); fees vary 100-fold between devices.

Think of it like…

Braket is like a car-rental marketplace: one account and one set of controls, but you can choose between several manufacturers' vehicles and pay per trip.

Real-world example

Diego, a cloud engineer at fictional Andes Logistics, tests a Bell circuit on Braket's free LocalSimulator, then prices a 1,000-shot run: IonQ Forte costs $0.30 + 1,000 × $0.08 = $80.30, IQM Garnet $0.30 + $1.45 = $1.75, and Rigetti Cepheus about $0.73. He uses the cheap devices for debugging and reserves IonQ for the final high-fidelity run.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. pip install amazon-braket-sdk; build circuits with braket.circuits.Circuit.
  2. Run locally with LocalSimulator (free) to check results.
  3. Configure AWS credentials, choose a device ARN and an S3 location for results.
  4. Submit a quantum task with device.run(circuit, shots=N); track cost with the Braket cost Tracker.
  5. For iterative algorithms, package code as a Hybrid Job, or book dedicated time with Braket Direct reservations.

Who uses it

AWS-based enterprises, researchers comparing hardware modalities, and teams who want one SDK across multiple vendors without separate contracts.

Key takeaway

Memorise the pricing shape: $0.30 per task plus a device-specific per-shot fee; managed simulators bill per minute (SV1 at $0.075/min).

Going deeper

  • Braket's 2026 on-demand QPUs include IonQ Forte, IQM Garnet and Emerald, Rigetti Cepheus, AQT IBEX-Q1 and QuEra Aquila (analog Hamiltonian simulation); every task costs $0.30 plus a per-shot fee from $0.000425 (Rigetti) to $0.08 (IonQ).
  • Managed simulators: SV1 (state vector, up to 34 qubits), DM1 (density matrix with noise, up to 17 qubits) and TN1 (tensor network, up to 50 qubits); SV1 is billed at $0.075 per minute in 1 ms increments with a 3-second minimum.
  • Braket uses OpenQASM 3 as an input format, supports 'verbatim' boxes that bypass compilation for pulse-level-like control of native gates, and returns results to an Amazon S3 bucket.
  • Hybrid Jobs run your classical code in a managed container with priority QPU access; embedded simulators such as PennyLane Lightning inside a job cost only the instance time (e.g. ml.m5.xlarge).
  • Braket Direct lets teams reserve a whole QPU by the hour (for example IonQ Forte at $7,000/hour or IQM Garnet at $3,000/hour in 2026 list prices) and offers expert consultation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Forgetting per-shot fees scale linearly: 100,000 shots on IonQ Forte cost about $8,000, so prototype on simulators and cheap devices first.
  • Assuming every device supports every gate or feature: check device.properties for native gates, connectivity and mid-circuit measurement support.
  • Leaving results in S3 with broad permissions: quantum results are ordinary cloud data and need normal access controls.

docs.title: 6.9 pytket, Guppy, Quantinuum Nexus and Other SDKs
docs.text:
Beyond the big four frameworks, many specialised tools exist. Quantinuum offers TKET (pytket), a hardware-agnostic compiler, plus Guppy, a Python-embedded language for programs with real-time classical control, the Selene emulator and the Nexus cloud platform. Other SDKs serve specific hardware (pyQuil for Rigetti, Pulser for Pasqal, Perceval for photonics, Ocean for D-Wave) or offer higher-level design (Classiq, Qrisp).

The wider SDK landscape. Pick tools by layer: high-level design, general frameworks, compilers, and hardware-specific SDKs.

Think of it like…

It's like the world of programming languages: most people start with Python or Java, but specialists reach for tools built for their exact job — embedded C for microcontrollers, SQL for databases.

Real-world example

Mei, a developer at fictional Aurora Pharma, compiles a chemistry circuit with pytket's optimisation passes and saves 18% of two-qubit gates compared with her first draft. For Quantinuum's Helios she rewrites an adaptive measurement routine in Guppy, tests it on the Selene emulator through Nexus, and only then submits it to hardware.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a tool by goal: compilation (pytket), adaptive programs (Guppy), high-level synthesis (Classiq, Qrisp) or hardware-specific SDKs.
  2. Install the SDK and its extensions (e.g. pytket-qiskit or pytket-quantinuum).
  3. Write or import circuits, often from Qiskit or OpenQASM, and compile with the tool's passes.
  4. Test on an emulator or simulator that models the target device.
  5. Submit through the vendor's cloud (Nexus, Rigetti QCS, Pasqal Cloud, D-Wave Leap) or a multi-vendor service.

Who uses it

Developers targeting specific hardware vendors, compiler researchers, optimisation teams using annealers, and enterprises evaluating high-level quantum design platforms.

Key takeaway

Know at least one non-IBM toolchain end to end — interviewers like candidates who can explain why different hardware needs different software.

Going deeper

  • TKET is an optimising compiler with routing, gate-synthesis and peephole passes; pytket 2.18 was current in October 2026, with extensions connecting it to Qiskit, Cirq, Braket, Quantinuum and other back ends.
  • Guppy (guppylang 1.x) is an open-source, statically typed language embedded in Python that supports loops, conditionals and functions driven by mid-circuit measurements; Guppy programs compile to HUGR, Quantinuum's hierarchical intermediate representation.
  • Quantinuum Nexus is the cloud platform for its Helios and H-series machines, handling jobs, data, team projects and access to emulators including Selene, which offers state-vector, stabiliser and GPU-accelerated tensor-network back ends.
  • Classiq (classiq 1.31) and Qrisp (0.9, from Fraunhofer FOKUS) raise the abstraction level: you describe functions, variables and constraints, and the tool synthesises or manages the underlying circuits and ancilla qubits.
  • Hardware SDKs expose native capabilities: pyQuil/Quil for Rigetti's QCS, Pulser for pulse-level neutral-atom sequences on Pasqal, Bloqade for QuEra, Perceval for Quandela's photonics, and Ocean for D-Wave annealing (not gate-model).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every SDK targets every machine: D-Wave's Ocean is for annealers and won't run gate circuits; Pulser describes pulses, not gates.
  • Ignoring version churn: young SDKs like Guppy change syntax between releases, so pin versions and follow migration notes.
  • Choosing a high-level platform without checking export options: make sure you can get OpenQASM or another standard format out if you change vendors.

docs.title: 6.10 OpenQASM 3, QIR and Interchange Formats
docs.text:
Interchange formats are shared languages that let quantum programs move between tools and hardware. OpenQASM is a text format for circuits — version 3 adds classical logic, loops, timing and subroutines. QIR (Quantum Intermediate Representation) is a lower-level format based on LLVM, used by compilers for programs with complex classical control. Using standards keeps your work portable across vendors.

How programs travel between tools. Standard formats are the hand-off points between front ends, compilers and hardware.

Think of it like…

OpenQASM is like a PDF of your circuit — readable and portable; QIR is like a compiled machine-independent bytecode — less readable, but ready for many different compilers to consume.

Real-world example

Kwame, a consultant at fictional Bridgeline Advisory, exports a client's Qiskit circuit with qasm3.dumps and sends the text file to a colleague using Amazon Braket, which accepts OpenQASM 3 directly. Another teammate compiles the same OpenQASM through Microsoft's QDK to QIR to submit on an Azure Quantum target. One circuit, three ecosystems, no manual rewriting.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write or export a circuit in OpenQASM 3 (e.g. qiskit.qasm3.dumps).
  2. Validate it with a parser such as the openqasm3 reference package.
  3. Import it into another SDK or submit it directly to services that accept OpenQASM (Braket, Azure Quantum, IBM).
  4. For programs with rich classical control, compile to QIR with a tool such as the QDK or CUDA-Q.
  5. Keep the source format in version control alongside a binary snapshot (e.g. QPY) for exact reproducibility.

Who uses it

Compiler engineers, SDK maintainers, consultants moving workloads between vendors, and anyone archiving experiments in a vendor-neutral format.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: OpenQASM 3 for human-readable portable circuits; QIR for compiled programs with classical control; QPY for exact Qiskit round-trips.

Going deeper

  • OpenQASM 2.0 (Cross et al., 2017) described static circuits; OpenQASM 3 (Cross et al., ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing, 2022) adds typed classical variables, if/while/for, subroutines, extern calls, timing with delay and box, and pulse-level calibration through OpenPulse.
  • OpenQASM is governed by a Technical Steering Committee with members from several companies; the openqasm3 Python package (1.0.1) provides the reference abstract syntax tree and parser.
  • QIR builds on LLVM IR, so standard compiler infrastructure can optimise classical parts; the QIR Alliance, hosted under the Linux Foundation's Joint Development Foundation, maintains the specification and profiles such as Base and Adaptive.
  • Qiskit's qasm3.dumps exports natively, while qasm3.loads relies on the separate qiskit-qasm3-import package; QPY is Qiskit's binary format that round-trips every circuit detail including parameters and layouts.
  • Newer intermediate representations target error-corrected, hybrid programs: Quantinuum's HUGR (from Guppy), MLIR-based dialects in CUDA-Q (Quake) and PennyLane Catalyst, all designed for loops and real-time control.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every OpenQASM 3 feature is supported everywhere: many back ends accept only a subset (often no while loops or extern calls).
  • Confusing OpenQASM 2 and 3 files: the header line and gate libraries differ, and some tools accept only one version.
  • Treating QIR as a human-readable format: it is compiler output; keep a higher-level source for review and editing.

docs.title: 6.11 Quantum Simulators: Methods, Limits and GPUs
docs.text:
Simulators run quantum circuits on ordinary computers, which is how almost all development and testing happens. A full state-vector simulator stores 2ⁿ complex numbers, so each added qubit doubles the memory: 30 qubits need 16 GiB, 40 qubits about 16 TiB. Specialised methods — stabiliser, tensor-network, matrix-product-state and density-matrix simulators — trade generality for much larger or noisier circuits.

State-vector memory doubles per qubit. Double-precision complex amplitudes (16 bytes each); note the log scale — 50 qubits needs 16 PiB.

Think of it like…

A state-vector simulator is like keeping a full spreadsheet of every possible lottery outcome — fine for a small lottery, impossible for a big one; tensor-network and stabiliser methods are clever shortcuts that work only when the lottery has hidden structure.

Real-world example

Farah, a PhD student, needs a 500-qubit GHZ state for a networking study. A state vector would need 2⁵⁰⁰ amplitudes — impossible — but Qiskit Aer's stabiliser method samples it in a fraction of a second because the circuit uses only H and CNOT, and the MPS method also succeeds because entanglement stays low. For a 28-qubit chemistry circuit with T gates she switches to a GPU state vector.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Classify the circuit: Clifford-only? low entanglement? noisy? number of qubits?
  2. Pick a method: stabiliser for Clifford, MPS/tensor network for low entanglement, state vector for general circuits up to ~30-40 qubits.
  3. Use density-matrix or trajectory (Monte Carlo) simulation when you need noise.
  4. Move to GPUs (cuQuantum, Aer GPU, lightning.gpu, CUDA-Q) or clusters when memory or speed limits bite.
  5. Validate small cases against an exact simulator before trusting approximate methods at scale.

Who uses it

Every quantum developer, plus HPC centres and researchers verifying 'quantum advantage' claims with classical simulation.

Key takeaway

Memorise: memory = 2ⁿ × 16 bytes for double-precision state vectors — 30 qubits = 16 GiB, 40 qubits = 16 TiB, 50 qubits = 16 PiB; density matrices square that (4ⁿ).

Going deeper

  • Stabiliser simulators rely on the Gottesman-Knill theorem and Aaronson-Gottesman tableaus (2004), costing polynomial time; Stim and Aer's stabilizer method handle thousands of qubits, while 'extended stabiliser' methods add a few T gates at exponential cost in T-count.
  • Matrix product states store the state as a chain of tensors whose bond dimension grows with entanglement; they excel on 1D-like, shallow or low-entanglement circuits and were used to challenge several quantum-advantage claims.
  • Density-matrix simulation needs 4ⁿ entries (16 GiB at 15 qubits), so noisy simulation of larger circuits usually uses quantum trajectories: many state-vector runs with randomly sampled errors.
  • NVIDIA's cuQuantum SDK (cuStateVec, cuTensorNet, cuDensityMat; cuquantum-python 26.9 in 2026) accelerates Qiskit Aer, PennyLane Lightning, CUDA-Q, qsim and others; single-precision halves memory (8 bytes per amplitude).
  • Managed cloud simulators have published limits: Braket SV1 up to 34 qubits, DM1 17 qubits, TN1 50 qubits; Google says qsim reaches about 40 qubits on a 90-core workstation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing 'a simulator can't do more than 50 qubits': for Clifford, low-entanglement or shallow circuits, specialised methods go far beyond.
  • Trusting a noiseless simulator's results as a hardware prediction: add a realistic noise model or fake backend before estimating real-device performance.
  • Running density-matrix simulations by default: they hit memory limits at about half the qubits of a state vector; use trajectories instead.

docs.title: Try it: Simulate a 500-qubit GHZ state with stabiliser and MPS methods (pip install qiskit qiskit-aer)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

n = 500
ghz = QuantumCircuit(n); ghz.h(0)
for i in range(n - 1):
    ghz.cx(i, i + 1)
ghz.measure_all()

for method in ["stabilizer", "matrix_product_state"]:
    counts = AerSimulator(method=method).run(ghz, shots=4).result().get_counts()
    print(method, {k[:6] + "...": v for k, v in counts.items()})
# A statevector simulation of 500 qubits would need 2**500 amplitudes - impossible.

docs.title: 6.12 Cloud Access and Pricing Models
docs.text:
Almost nobody owns a quantum computer; you rent time over the cloud. IBM sells QPU minutes on its own platform, AWS Braket and Azure Quantum act as marketplaces for several vendors, and companies such as IonQ, Quantinuum, Rigetti, IQM and Pasqal also offer direct access. Prices are measured in different units — QPU seconds, shots, tasks or credits — so comparing costs takes care.

Three major cloud routes to QPUs

IBM Quantum Platform Amazon Braket Azure Quantum Hardware IBM superconducting QPUs IonQ, IQM, Rigetti, AQT, QuEra IonQ, Quantinuum, Pasqal, Rigetti Billing unit QPU time (seconds) Per task + per shot Per provider's pricing Example rate $96/min Pay-As-You-Go $0.30/task + $0.00145-0.08/shot Varies by provider plan Free option Open Plan: 10 min / 28 days Free local simulators Free local QDK simulators Main SDK Qiskit Braket SDK (+ plugins) QDK / Q#, Qiskit, Cirq

Billing units differ; normalise to cost per experiment before comparing.

Think of it like…

It is like comparing mobile-phone plans: some charge by the minute, some by the message, some sell bundles of credits — the cheapest choice depends on how you use it.

Real-world example

Hannah, a project lead at fictional Northwind Bank, budgets a pilot: IBM's Pay-As-You-Go rate is $96 per QPU minute, so 100 experiments of about 6 seconds each cost about $960. The same 1,000-shot circuits on IonQ Forte via Braket would cost $80.30 each, or $8,030 in total, but on IQM Garnet only $175. She runs development on simulators and free tiers, then buys a small amount of the hardware that matches her technical needs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what hardware properties you need (qubit count, connectivity, fidelity, mid-circuit measurement).
  2. List providers offering that hardware and their billing units (seconds, shots, tasks, credits).
  3. Estimate usage: circuits × shots × repetitions, including error-mitigation overhead.
  4. Use free tiers, credits and simulators for development; reserve paid QPU time for final runs.
  5. Track spending with provider dashboards and cost tools; set budgets and alerts.

Who uses it

Project managers, researchers writing grant budgets, enterprise innovation teams and students looking for free access all need to understand quantum cloud pricing.

Key takeaway

Always convert prices to 'cost per useful result' — a cheaper but noisier device may need far more shots or mitigation to reach the same answer quality.

Going deeper

  • IBM's 2026 prices: Open Plan free (10 minutes per 28 days), Pay-As-You-Go $96/minute billed per second, Flex $72/minute (400-minute minimum), Premium from $48/minute (5,200+ minutes a year), on-premises by quote.
  • Braket charges $0.30 per task plus device per-shot fees (e.g. IonQ Forte $0.08, IQM Garnet $0.00145, Rigetti Cepheus $0.000425) and offers hourly Braket Direct reservations from about $2,500 to $7,000 per hour depending on the device.
  • Quantinuum prices its machines in H-System Quantum Credits (HQCs), computed from gate and measurement counts, usually through subscriptions; IonQ and others sell direct cloud access alongside marketplace listings.
  • Google does not sell public access to its processors; in 2026 it ran a Willow Early Access Program for selected research proposals, while its software (Cirq, qsim, Stim) is freely available.
  • Dedicated and on-premises systems are a growing model: IBM Quantum System One/Two installations (e.g. at RIKEN and in Europe), and national centres buying their own machines for priority access and data sovereignty.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing per-shot prices without considering fidelity: a device needing 10× more shots or heavy mitigation may cost more overall.
  • Forgetting mitigation and transpilation overhead in budgets: twirling and ZNE can multiply QPU time several-fold.
  • Leaving credentials or unrestricted keys in shared code: a leaked API key can spend your quantum budget like any cloud key.
