docs.title: 2.4 Universal Gate Sets, Clifford+T and the Solovay-Kitaev Theorem
docs.text:
A gate set is universal if combining its gates can approximate any quantum operation as closely as you like. CNOT plus all single-qubit gates is universal, and so is the finite set {H, S, T, CNOT}, called Clifford+T. The Solovay-Kitaev theorem guarantees that this approximation is efficient: the number of gates grows only with a power of log(1/ε), where ε is the precision.

Compiling an arbitrary rotation for a fault-tolerant machine. Precision costs gates: each extra decimal digit adds roughly 10 T gates with gridsynth.

Think of it like…

A universal gate set is like a small box of Lego bricks from which you can build any shape to any precision — finer detail just needs more bricks, and Solovay-Kitaev promises you will not need absurdly many.

Real-world example

Yusuf's fault-tolerant compiler can only run Clifford+T, but his algorithm needs RZ(0.3). Qiskit's Solovay-Kitaev pass approximates it with about 46 H/T/T† gates at error 0.05, rising to about 900 gates at error 0.006. A specialised number-theoretic method (gridsynth) does far better, needing only about 3·log2(1/ε) T gates.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Single-qubit gates plus CNOT can build any n-qubit unitary exactly (Barenco et al., 1995).
  2. Real hardware uses a finite gate set, so arbitrary rotations must be approximated to precision ε.
  3. Clifford gates (H, S, CNOT) alone are not universal and are classically simulable (Gottesman-Knill).
  4. Adding T makes the set universal; H and T generate a dense set of single-qubit rotations.
  5. Solovay-Kitaev: any gate is approximated with O(log^c(1/ε)) gates, with c about 3.97 originally, later reduced to about 1.44.

Who uses it

Fault-tolerance researchers, compiler and synthesis engineers, and resource-estimation teams live with Clifford+T and T-counts.

Key takeaway

Interview soundbite: 'Clifford+T is universal; Cliffords are cheap and simulable, T gates are expensive and give the quantum power — so we count T gates.'

Going deeper

  • Solovay (unpublished, 1995) and Kitaev (1997) proved the theorem; Dawson and Nielsen's 2005 tutorial gave the standard algorithm with gate count O(log^3.97(1/ε)).
  • Greg Kuperberg's 2023 paper 'Breaking the cubic barrier in the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm' lowered the exponent to about 1.44 (log base golden ratio of 2) for general gate sets.
  • For Clifford+T specifically, number-theoretic synthesis (Kliuchnikov-Maslov-Mosca 2013; Ross-Selinger gridsynth 2016) is near-optimal, using about 3·log2(1/ε) + O(log log(1/ε)) T gates per Z rotation.
  • The Gottesman-Knill theorem (1998) shows circuits of Cliffords, Pauli measurements and computational-basis inputs are simulable in polynomial time; Stim simulates millions of such qubit-operations per second.
  • Most unitaries need exponentially many gates: a counting argument (Knill 1995) shows almost all n-qubit unitaries require on the order of 4^n gates, so useful algorithms are special, structured circuits.
  • Other universal sets include {Toffoli, H} (real amplitudes only, Shi 2003), {CCZ, H} and {CNOT, H, T}; hardware native sets such as {RZ, SX, CZ} are universal with continuous angles.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking universal means exact: finite sets only approximate most gates, with cost growing as precision tightens.
  • Ignoring T-count when estimating fault-tolerant runtimes; T gates usually dominate time and qubit overhead.
  • Believing Clifford-only circuits can show quantum advantage: they are efficiently simulable classically.

docs.title: Try it: Approximate RZ(0.3) with only H, T and T† using Solovay-Kitaev (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.transpiler.passes import SolovayKitaev
from qiskit.quantum_info import Operator

qc = QuantumCircuit(1); qc.rz(0.3, 0)
for depth in (1, 2, 3):
    approx = SolovayKitaev(recursion_degree=depth)(qc)
    err = np.linalg.norm(Operator(approx).data - Operator(qc).data, 2)
    print(depth, sum(approx.count_ops().values()), 'gates, error', round(err, 4))

Stim and stabiliser simulatorsCraig Gidney (Stim, 2021) · Tool · Current · Intermediate Fast Clifford-circuit simulators exploiting Gottesman-Knill, used for error-correction research. Stim samples surface-code circuits with thousands of qubits at millions of shots per minute.

docs.title: 2.5 The Circuit Model: Reading Diagrams, Depth, Width and Gate Counts
docs.text:
A quantum circuit is a recipe drawn as horizontal wires (one per qubit) with gates placed on them from left to right, ending with measurements. Width is the number of qubits, depth is the number of time steps when gates that can run in parallel share a step, and gate counts — especially two-qubit gates — estimate how much noise the circuit will suffer.

A 3-qubit GHZ circuit, layer by layer. Gates on different qubits in the same layer run in parallel; depth here is 4.

Think of it like…

A circuit diagram is like a musical score: each wire is an instrument's staff, gates are notes, notes stacked vertically play together, and depth is how long the piece lasts.

Real-world example

Zainab writes a 5-qubit GHZ circuit: one H, then four CNOTs in a chain. Width is 5, depth 5, and the two-qubit count 4. She rewrites it as a tree — qubit 0 entangles 1, then 0 and 1 each entangle another, and so on — cutting depth to 4 here and to about log2(n) for large n, which matters on hardware where qubits decohere while waiting.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Draw one wire per qubit (top wire is qubit 0 in most tools) and double lines for classical bits.
  2. Place gates left to right in time order; boxes span the qubits they act on, with dots marking controls.
  3. Group gates that touch disjoint qubits into the same layer (a 'moment' in Cirq).
  4. Depth = number of layers on the longest path; width = number of qubits (plus classical bits in some tools).
  5. Report gate counts by type; two-qubit gate count and two-qubit depth best predict errors on NISQ hardware.

Who uses it

Developers read circuit diagrams daily; benchmarking engineers and resource estimators track depth, width and gate counts.

Key takeaway

Quote three numbers for any circuit: qubits, two-qubit gate count and two-qubit depth — measured after transpiling to the target hardware.

Going deeper

  • The circuit model was formalised by Deutsch (1989) and Yao (1993), who showed quantum circuits are equivalent to quantum Turing machines with polynomial overhead.
  • Uniformity matters for complexity theory: a family of circuits, one per input size, must be generated by an efficient classical program, otherwise circuits could hide answers.
  • Two-qubit depth is often more meaningful than total depth because single-qubit gates are fast and accurate, and RZ gates are often free virtual operations.
  • Practical limits in 2025-2026: IBM rated Nighthawk for circuits of about 5,000 two-qubit gates with a target of 7,500 by end-2026; trapped-ion machines run fewer, slower but higher-fidelity gates.
  • Circuit cutting (Qiskit addon) splits a wide circuit into smaller pieces run separately and recombined classically, at a sampling cost that grows exponentially with the number of cuts.
  • Cirq structures circuits explicitly as Moments, Qiskit as a DAG of instructions; both export OpenQASM for interchange between tools.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting depth before transpilation: routing and native-gate translation can multiply depth several times.
  • Mixing qubit-ordering conventions when reading diagrams and bitstrings (Qiskit's top wire is qubit 0 but the rightmost bit).
  • Assuming barriers are free: they block optimisations and can increase depth.

docs.title: Try it: Measure a circuit's width, depth and gate counts (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(5)
qc.h(0)
for t in range(1, 5):
    qc.cx(t - 1, t)                     # chain GHZ
qc.measure_all()
print(qc.draw())
print('width', qc.num_qubits, 'depth', qc.depth())
print(qc.count_ops(), 'two-qubit:', qc.num_nonlocal_gates())

docs.title: 2.6 Measurement, Mid-Circuit Measurement and Classical Feed-Forward
docs.text:
Most simple circuits measure all qubits once, at the end. Modern hardware can also measure some qubits in the middle of a circuit, reset them for reuse, and use the result immediately to decide which gates come next — called classical feed-forward or 'dynamic circuits'. This is essential for teleportation, error correction and many efficient algorithms.

Feed-forward inside one shot. The classical decision must finish before the waiting qubits decohere.

Think of it like…

A static circuit is a recorded speech played start to finish; a dynamic circuit is a live interview where the next question depends on the last answer.

Real-world example

Hiro's team at the fictional Kestrel Labs needs a 50-qubit GHZ state but long CNOT chains are noisy. Using mid-circuit measurements and feed-forward they build small GHZ blocks in parallel, measure the joining qubits, and apply X corrections conditioned on the results, achieving constant-depth preparation on hardware that supports fast conditional operations.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Run gates as usual up to the point where information is needed.
  2. Measure selected qubits mid-circuit, storing outcomes in classical bits while others stay coherent.
  3. The control system evaluates a classical condition (if/else, switch, loops) in real time.
  4. Apply conditional gates, such as a Pauli correction, or reset measured qubits for reuse.
  5. Continue the circuit; all of this must happen well within the remaining qubits' coherence time.

Who uses it

Error-correction engineers, protocol designers (teleportation, entanglement distillation) and control-system/FPGA engineers build on dynamic circuits.

Key takeaway

Know the deferred measurement principle: any mid-circuit measurement used for control can be replaced by a quantum-controlled gate and a measurement at the end — useful when hardware lacks feed-forward.

Going deeper

  • OpenQASM 3 added real-time classical control — if/else, while and for loops, switch statements, classical arithmetic and timing — specifically to express dynamic circuits portably.
  • Feed-forward latency on superconducting systems is typically hundreds of nanoseconds to a few microseconds including readout, which consumes a noticeable fraction of a 100-300 µs coherence budget.
  • Mid-circuit measurement can disturb neighbouring idle qubits through measurement-induced dephasing and crosstalk; trapped-ion and neutral-atom systems often shuttle qubits away or shield them during readout.
  • Quantinuum's QCCD trapped-ion systems have supported mid-circuit measurement, reset and conditional logic since the H1 generation, making them common hosts for error-correction demonstrations.
  • Measurement plus feed-forward can create long-range entanglement in constant depth, outperforming unitary-only circuits whose depth must grow with distance on local hardware.
  • Error-correction cycles are dynamic circuits at scale: ancillas are measured every round (about 1 µs on Google Willow), reset and reused thousands of times.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every backend supports conditional gates: check the target's dynamic-circuit support before relying on if_test.
  • Ignoring the latency cost: waiting for feed-forward exposes idle qubits to decoherence, so add dynamical decoupling.
  • Forgetting that resetting a qubit without measuring can leave residual excitation; check the reset fidelity.

docs.title: Try it: A dynamic circuit: measure, then flip another qubit only if the result was 1 (Qiskit 2.x + qiskit-aer)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator      # pip install qiskit-aer

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)                         # mid-circuit measurement
with qc.if_test((qc.clbits[0], 1)):      # classical feed-forward
    qc.x(1)
qc.measure(1, 1)
print(AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=1000).result().get_counts())
# only '00' and '11' - qubit 1 copies the classical result

docs.title: 2.7 Preparing Bell, GHZ and W States
docs.text:
Entangled states are built with short, standard circuits. An H followed by a CNOT makes a Bell state; extra X or Z gates select which of the four Bell states you get. Chaining CNOTs spreads the entanglement into a GHZ state, (|00…0⟩ + |11…1⟩)/√2, while a W state shares a single 1 evenly among qubits, (|100⟩ + |010⟩ + |001⟩)/√3. These states are the 'hello world' and the benchmarks of quantum hardware.

GHZ vs W entanglement

GHZ state W state 3-qubit form (|000⟩ + |111⟩)/√2 (|001⟩ + |010⟩ + |100⟩)/√3 Basic circuit H + CNOT chain RY + controlled-H + CNOTs Lose one qubit Others unentangled Others stay entangled Typical use Benchmarks, sensing Robust networks Stabilisers XXX, ZZI, IZZ Not a stabiliser state

Both are 3-qubit entangled states, but they behave very differently under loss.

Think of it like…

A GHZ state is a group of dancers who either all sit or all stand — one person leaving ruins the pattern. A W state is a single torch passed around a circle: lose one person and the others still share the flame.

Real-world example

Olu benchmarks a new chip at the fictional Aurora Quantum Lab. He prepares GHZ states of growing size and measures fidelity using parity oscillations. Fidelity stays above 0.5 — the threshold proving genuine multi-qubit entanglement — up to 24 qubits on the first chip but beyond 40 on the next, a clear sign of better two-qubit gates.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Φ+: H on q0, CNOT(q0→q1) gives (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.
  2. Φ−: add Z on q0; Ψ+: add X on q1; Ψ−: add both, giving (|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2.
  3. GHZ on n qubits: H on q0, then CNOTs to each other qubit (chain or tree, depth about log2 n for a tree).
  4. W on 3 qubits: RY(2·arccos(1/√3)) on q0, controlled-H to q1, then CNOTs and an X to spread one excitation.
  5. Verify with populations (only 00…0 and 11…1 for GHZ) plus parity or stabiliser measurements to confirm coherence.

Who uses it

Hardware benchmarking teams, quantum-networking engineers and students use these states to test gates, links and entanglement.

Key takeaway

The Bell measurement is the Bell-state circuit run backwards: CNOT, then H, then measure both qubits — remember it for teleportation and superdense coding.

Going deeper

  • Greenberger, Horne and Zeilinger introduced GHZ states in 1989; Mermin's 1990 analysis showed they contradict local realism in a single run, not just statistically like Bell tests.
  • GHZ and W states cannot be converted into each other even probabilistically using local operations and classical communication (Dür, Vidal and Cirac, 2000), so they are two distinct classes of three-qubit entanglement.
  • GHZ fidelity is estimated from populations P(00…0) + P(11…1) plus the amplitude of parity oscillations when every qubit is rotated by a phase; F > 0.5 certifies genuine n-qubit entanglement.
  • An n-qubit GHZ state is sensitive to dephasing n times faster than a single qubit, which makes it useful for Heisenberg-limited sensing and a tough benchmark for hardware.
  • The four Bell states form an orthonormal basis of two qubits; a Bell-state measurement distinguishes all four with CNOT, H and two Z measurements on gate-based hardware.
  • Dicke states generalise W states to k excitations shared among n qubits; deterministic preparation circuits (Bärtschi and Eidenbenz, 2019) use O(kn) gates.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Checking only the 00…0 and 11…1 counts: a classical mixture gives the same populations; coherence needs parity measurements.
  • Building large GHZ states with a linear CNOT chain on hardware: tree or measurement-assisted constructions are much shallower.
  • Assuming W and GHZ are interchangeable: their robustness and uses differ fundamentally.

docs.title: Try it: Build a 3-qubit W state and check its amplitudes (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

w = QuantumCircuit(3)
w.ry(2 * np.arccos(1 / np.sqrt(3)), 0)
w.ch(0, 1)
w.cx(1, 2)
w.cx(0, 1)
w.x(0)
print(Statevector(w).probabilities_dict())
# {'001': 0.333, '010': 0.333, '100': 0.333}

An n-qubit GHZ oscillates n times faster in phase than a single qubit, confirming genuine entanglement. GHZ fidelity above 0.5 is a widely used witness of genuine n-qubit entanglement.

docs.title: 2.8 Quantum Teleportation and Superdense Coding
docs.text:
Teleportation moves an unknown qubit state from Alice to Bob using one shared Bell pair plus two ordinary classical bits — nothing travels faster than light, and Alice's original is destroyed. Superdense coding is the mirror image: by sending one qubit of a shared Bell pair, Alice delivers two classical bits to Bob. Both show entanglement acting as a communication resource.

Quantum teleportation. Only two classical bits travel after the Bell pair is shared; the state itself is never copied.

Think of it like…

Teleportation is like sending a locked safe's contents using a pre-shared set of matching keys: Alice's two-bit 'which key' note travels by normal post, and only with it can Bob rebuild the original — while Alice's copy self-destructs.

Real-world example

In a fictional network test, Alice in Leeds holds a qubit in an unknown state and shares a Bell pair with Bob in Manchester. She performs a Bell measurement on her two qubits, getting 1 and 0, and sends '10' over the internet. Bob applies Z, and his qubit now holds the original state exactly. Had he guessed without the bits, he would have had only a 25% chance of applying the right correction.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Teleportation: Alice and Bob share Φ+; Alice also holds the unknown state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩.
  2. Alice applies CNOT (ψ-qubit → her half), then H on the ψ-qubit, and measures both: bits m1, m2.
  3. She sends m1 m2 classically; Bob applies X^(m2) then Z^(m1) and holds |ψ⟩.
  4. Superdense coding: Alice applies I, X, Z or ZX to her half of Φ+ to encode 00, 01, 10 or 11, and sends her qubit.
  5. Bob performs a Bell measurement on both qubits and reads the two bits with certainty.

Who uses it

Quantum-network engineers, QEC designers (gate teleportation, lattice surgery) and students use these as core protocols.

Key takeaway

Resource accounting to memorise: teleportation = 1 ebit + 2 classical bits → 1 qubit; superdense coding = 1 ebit + 1 qubit → 2 classical bits.

Going deeper

  • Teleportation was proposed in 1993 by Bennett, Brassard, Crépeau, Jozsa, Peres and Wootters; the first photonic demonstrations came in 1997 from Innsbruck (Zeilinger's group) and Rome (De Martini's group).
  • China's Micius satellite teleported photon qubits from a ground station in Tibet to orbit over distances up to about 1,400 km in 2017, a landmark for space-based quantum networks.
  • Superdense coding was proposed by Bennett and Wiesner in 1992 and demonstrated with photons in 1996 by Mattle, Weinfurter, Kwiat and Zeilinger, though linear optics could distinguish only three of the four Bell states.
  • Gate teleportation (Gottesman and Chuang, 1999) applies a gate by teleporting through a pre-prepared resource state; it underlies magic-state injection, measurement-based computing and modular architectures.
  • Entanglement swapping teleports entanglement itself: Bell-measuring one qubit from each of two pairs entangles the two far ends, the core of quantum repeaters (applications chapter).
  • Teleportation fidelity above 2/3 beats the best classical measure-and-prepare strategy for unknown qubit states, so experiments report fidelity against that benchmark.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Claiming teleportation sends information faster than light: Bob's qubit is useless until the classical bits arrive.
  • Thinking teleportation copies the state: Alice's original is destroyed by her measurement, respecting no-cloning.
  • Assuming superdense coding beats channel capacity for free: it needs one pre-shared ebit per two bits sent.

docs.title: Try it: Teleport the state RY(1.1)|0> with mid-circuit measurement and feed-forward (Qiskit 2.x + qiskit-aer)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
qc.ry(1.1, 0)                      # unknown state on q0 (P(1) ~ 0.27)
qc.h(1); qc.cx(1, 2)               # Bell pair: q1 Alice, q2 Bob
qc.cx(0, 1); qc.h(0)               # Alice's Bell measurement
qc.measure(0, 0); qc.measure(1, 1)
with qc.if_test((qc.clbits[1], 1)):
    qc.x(2)
with qc.if_test((qc.clbits[0], 1)):
    qc.z(2)
qc.measure(2, 2)
counts = AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=4000).result().get_counts()
ones = sum(v for k, v in counts.items() if k[0] == '1')
print('P(Bob=1) =', ones / 4000)   # ~0.27, matching the original

docs.title: 2.9 Phase Kickback, the Hadamard Test and the Swap Test
docs.text:
When a controlled gate acts on a target that is already an eigenstate of the gate, the target does not change — instead the gate's phase is 'kicked back' onto the control qubit. That turns hidden information (a phase) into something measurable after a Hadamard. Phase kickback powers Deutsch-Jozsa, phase estimation and Shor's algorithm, and the Hadamard and swap tests are two everyday tools built on it.

Phase kickback in five moves. The target never changes; the phase moves to the control and becomes measurable.

Think of it like…

It is like pushing a heavy wall: the wall (target eigenstate) does not move, so you are the one who gets pushed back. Measuring how far you moved tells you how hard the wall pushed.

Real-world example

Marta puts the target qubit in |−⟩, an eigenstate of X with eigenvalue −1, and the control in |+⟩. After a CNOT the target is still |−⟩, but the control has become |−⟩ — the −1 moved to the control. A final H on the control turns |−⟩ into |1⟩, so she reads 1 with certainty, detecting the phase without ever measuring the target.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Prepare the target in an eigenstate |u⟩ of U with U|u⟩ = e^(iφ)|u⟩.
  2. Put the control in |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2.
  3. Apply controlled-U: the state becomes (|0⟩ + e^(iφ)|1⟩)/√2 ⊗ |u⟩ — the phase now sits on the control.
  4. Apply H to the control and measure: P(0) = (1 + cos φ)/2, revealing φ.
  5. Repeat with controlled-U^(2^k) and several controls to read φ bit by bit (phase estimation, algorithms chapter).

Who uses it

Algorithm designers and students of oracle algorithms, phase estimation and quantum chemistry energy estimation use kickback constantly.

Key takeaway

Exam favourite: a CNOT with target in |−⟩ acts as a Z on the control; with control and target both in the X basis the 'control' and 'target' roles reverse.

Going deeper

  • Cleve, Ekert, Macchiavello and Mosca (1998) unified Deutsch-Jozsa, Simon, Shor and phase estimation as phase-kickback plus Fourier-transform interference — a classic paper to read.
  • The Hadamard test estimates Re⟨ψ|U|ψ⟩ (and with an extra S† on the control, Im⟨ψ|U|ψ⟩) for any state, not just eigenstates, at the cost of many shots for precision ε (about 1/ε²).
  • The swap test uses a controlled-SWAP to estimate |⟨ψ|φ⟩|²: P(0) = (1 + |⟨ψ|φ⟩|²)/2, useful for state comparison and some quantum machine-learning kernels.
  • Phase oracles are built from bit oracles by kickback: with the target in |−⟩, |x⟩|−⟩ → (−1)^f(x)|x⟩|−⟩, which is exactly how Deutsch-Jozsa and Grover mark answers.
  • Iterative phase estimation reuses one control qubit with mid-circuit measurement and feed-forward, reading φ one bit per round instead of using many control qubits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing control qubits are never affected by controlled gates: kickback shows the control is often what changes.
  • Using a target that is not an eigenstate and expecting clean kickback: the control and target become entangled instead.
  • Forgetting shot costs: estimating a phase to precision ε with a Hadamard test needs on the order of 1/ε² repetitions.

docs.title: Try it: See phase kickback flip the control qubit (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.x(1); qc.h(1)           # target q1 = |->  (X eigenvalue -1)
qc.h(0)                    # control q0 = |+>
qc.cx(0, 1)                # phase -1 kicks back onto q0
qc.h(0)                    # |-> -> |1>
print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict(qargs=[0]))   # {'1': 1.0}

docs.title: 2.10 Density Matrices, Mixed States and the Partial Trace
docs.text:
State vectors describe qubits we know perfectly. Real qubits are noisy, and sometimes we only know a state with some probability — a mixed state. The density matrix ρ handles both cases: for a pure state ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ|, and for a mixture it is a probability-weighted sum. The partial trace lets you describe one part of a larger system on its own, which is how entanglement looks 'from the inside'.

What the density matrix ρ captures. One object describes pure states, noise, subsystems and measurement statistics.

Think of it like…

A state vector is a sharp photograph; a density matrix is that photo possibly blurred by camera shake. The partial trace is cropping a group photo to one person — you see them, but you lose how they were holding hands with the others.

Real-world example

Kwame's qubit should be |+⟩ but a noisy preparation gives |+⟩ 90% of the time and |−⟩ 10%. Its density matrix is ρ = 0.9|+⟩⟨+| + 0.1|−⟩⟨−| = [[0.5, 0.4],[0.4, 0.5]]. The off-diagonal 0.4 (instead of 0.5) is lost coherence; purity Tr(ρ²) = 0.82 instead of 1, and an X-basis measurement now gives '+' only 90% of the time.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pure state: ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ|; for |+⟩, ρ = ½[[1,1],[1,1]].
  2. Mixed state: ρ = Σ p_i |ψ_i⟩⟨ψ_i|; ρ is Hermitian, positive semidefinite, with trace 1.
  3. Diagonal entries are measurement probabilities; off-diagonal entries ('coherences') carry phase information.
  4. Single qubit: ρ = (I + r_x X + r_y Y + r_z Z)/2 with Bloch vector r, |r| ≤ 1 (|r| = 1 only when pure).
  5. Partial trace: for a Bell pair, tracing out qubit B leaves ρ_A = I/2 — maximally mixed, even though the pair is pure.

Who uses it

Noise modellers, error-correction researchers, hardware characterisation engineers and anyone simulating realistic devices use density matrices.

Key takeaway

Purity test: Tr(ρ²) = 1 for pure states and 1/d for the maximally mixed state of dimension d (½ for one qubit).

Going deeper

  • John von Neumann and Lev Landau introduced density matrices independently in 1927; von Neumann also defined the entropy S(ρ) = −Tr(ρ log2 ρ), which is 0 for pure states and n bits for n maximally mixed qubits.
  • Different ensembles can give the same ρ: an equal mix of |0⟩ and |1⟩ and an equal mix of |+⟩ and |−⟩ are both I/2 and are physically indistinguishable.
  • Expectation values are ⟨A⟩ = Tr(ρA) and outcome probabilities are p(k) = Tr(P_k ρ); measurement and noise act linearly on ρ, which is why simulators use it for noisy circuits.
  • Density-matrix simulation costs 4^n entries instead of 2^n, so exact noisy simulation tops out near 15-25 qubits on ordinary hardware, versus about 30 for state vectors on a laptop.
  • Every mixed state can be 'purified' as a pure state on a larger system; the partial trace runs that in reverse, and it is how decoherence is modelled as entanglement with the environment.
  • Distance measures include trace distance D(ρ, σ) = ½ Tr|ρ − σ|, the maximum bias for distinguishing two states, and Uhlmann fidelity, used to report gate and state quality.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating a 50/50 mixture as the same as the superposition |+⟩: the mixture has zero off-diagonal terms and gives random X-basis results.
  • Concluding a subsystem is 'noisy' because its reduced state is mixed: it may be perfectly entangled with another, pure subsystem.
  • Forgetting the 4^n cost when choosing a density-matrix simulator for large circuits.

docs.title: Try it: Density matrix, purity and partial trace of a Bell pair (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import DensityMatrix, partial_trace, entropy

bell = QuantumCircuit(2); bell.h(0); bell.cx(0, 1)
rho = DensityMatrix(bell)
print(rho.purity())                 # 1.0: the pair is pure
rho_a = partial_trace(rho, [1])     # trace out qubit 1
print(rho_a.data.real)              # [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]] = I/2
print(rho_a.purity(), entropy(rho_a))   # 0.5 and 1.0 bit

docs.title: 2.11 Noise Channels: Bit Flip, Phase Flip, Depolarising and Amplitude Damping
docs.text:
Noise is anything that changes a qubit in a way we did not intend. Physicists model it with quantum channels — rules that map a density matrix to a new one. The four standard models are bit flips (X errors), phase flips (Z errors), depolarising noise (the state is randomly scrambled) and amplitude damping (an excited |1⟩ decays to |0⟩, like a battery losing charge).

Three standard noise channels

Phase flip / dephasing Depolarising Amplitude damping Kraus operators √(1−p) I, √p Z I, X, Y, Z weighted E0, E1 (decay) Bloch ball effect Squash toward Z axis Shrink uniformly Shrink toward |0⟩ Changes populations? No Yes Yes Physical cause Flux / charge noise Many small errors Energy loss (T1) Linked metric T2 (Tφ) Gate error rate T1

Each channel shrinks or shifts the Bloch ball in a characteristic way.

Think of it like…

Think of a whispered message passed along a line: sometimes a word is swapped (bit flip), sometimes the tone changes so the meaning flips (phase flip), sometimes it becomes gibberish (depolarising), and sometimes the speaker simply runs out of breath and stops (amplitude damping).

Real-world example

Ana models a transmon with T1 = 200 µs. After an idle period of 20 µs, amplitude damping with γ = 1 − e^(−20/200) ≈ 0.095 means a qubit prepared in |1⟩ is found in |0⟩ about 9.5% of the time. She adds a depolarising error of 0.3% per CZ gate in Qiskit Aer and sees her 100-CZ circuit's success fall to roughly 0.997^100 ≈ 74%.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write the channel in operator-sum (Kraus) form: ρ → Σ_k E_k ρ E_k†, with Σ E_k†E_k = I.
  2. Bit flip: E0 = √(1−p) I, E1 = √p X. Phase flip: E0 = √(1−p) I, E1 = √p Z.
  3. Depolarising: ρ → (1−p)ρ + p·I/2 — the Bloch vector shrinks uniformly by (1−p).
  4. Amplitude damping: E0 = [[1,0],[0,√(1−γ)]], E1 = [[0,√γ],[0,0]], with γ = 1 − e^(−t/T1).
  5. Phase damping (pure dephasing) shrinks only off-diagonals; T2 combines both effects and satisfies T2 ≤ 2·T1.

Who uses it

Hardware characterisation engineers, error-correction and error-mitigation researchers, and developers building realistic simulations use these models.

Key takeaway

Interview fact: T1 is energy relaxation (|1⟩ → |0⟩); T2 is loss of phase coherence; T2 can never exceed 2·T1.

Going deeper

  • The operator-sum representation (Kraus, 1971/1983) and Choi's theorem (1975) characterise all physically allowed channels as completely positive, trace-preserving (CPTP) maps.
  • Markovian noise in continuous time obeys the Lindblad master equation (Lindblad; Gorini, Kossakowski and Sudarshan, 1976), whose jump operators generate amplitude damping and dephasing.
  • Coherent errors — systematic over-rotations such as RX(π + 0.01) instead of X — add up in amplitude, so errors can grow quadratically with gate count; randomised compiling (Pauli twirling) converts them into stochastic Pauli noise.
  • Leakage moves a qubit out of the {|0⟩, |1⟩} space, for example into a transmon's |2⟩ level or an atom lost from its trap; standard qubit channels miss it, and error correction needs special leakage-reduction steps.
  • Crosstalk and correlated errors (for example cosmic-ray bursts in superconducting chips) violate the independent-error assumption behind simple models and threshold proofs.
  • Qiskit Aer builds noise models from device calibration data (T1, T2, gate and readout errors), letting developers estimate hardware results before spending cloud credits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Modelling all noise as depolarising: real hardware has biased, coherent, leaky and correlated errors.
  • Confusing T2 with T2*: T2* (from Ramsey experiments) includes slow fluctuations that echo pulses can remove.
  • Assuming noise only acts during gates: idle qubits decohere too, which is why scheduling and decoupling matter.

docs.title: Try it: Apply amplitude damping as Kraus operators (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from qiskit.quantum_info import DensityMatrix, Kraus

gamma = 1 - np.exp(-20 / 200)         # 20 us idle, T1 = 200 us
E0 = np.array([[1, 0], [0, np.sqrt(1 - gamma)]])
E1 = np.array([[0, np.sqrt(gamma)], [0, 0]])
channel = Kraus([E0, E1])
rho = DensityMatrix.from_label('1').evolve(channel)
print(rho.probabilities())            # ~[0.095, 0.905]: decayed toward |0>

Error-correction simulations include Y errors because they trigger both X- and Z-type checks. Cosmic-ray impacts have caused bursts of correlated errors across many qubits of superconducting chips. docs.title: 2.12 Compilation and Transpilation: Native Gates, Qubit Routing and Connectivity
docs.text:
Real quantum chips understand only a few native gates, and each qubit can interact only with certain neighbours. A compiler — called a transpiler in Qiskit — rewrites your abstract circuit into native gates, chooses which physical qubits to use, inserts SWAP gates to bring distant qubits together, and optimises the result to minimise errors.

Qiskit's transpiler stages. Every stage preserves the circuit's meaning while fitting it to real hardware.

Think of it like…

Transpiling is like translating a speech into a local dialect and planning a delivery route through one-way streets: the meaning must stay the same, but the words and the route change to fit the place.

Real-world example

Liam's 5-qubit circuit has a CNOT from qubit 0 to each of the others, but his target chip connects qubits in a line. At optimisation level 0 the transpiler produces 13 CZ gates and depth 40; at level 3 it finds a smarter layout and needs only 10 CZs at depth 19. Since each CZ has about 0.3% error, that choice alone noticeably improves his results.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Init/unroll: break high-level operations (Toffoli, QFT blocks) into one- and two-qubit gates.
  2. Layout: map virtual qubits to physical qubits, preferring well-connected, low-error ones.
  3. Routing: insert SWAPs so every two-qubit gate acts on physically connected qubits.
  4. Translation: rewrite gates into the native basis, e.g. {RZ, SX, X, CZ} on IBM Heron.
  5. Optimisation and scheduling: cancel and merge gates, resynthesise blocks, and add timing such as dynamical decoupling.

Who uses it

Quantum software and compiler engineers, performance-minded developers and hardware-aware algorithm researchers work at this layer.

Key takeaway

Always inspect the transpiled circuit, not the logical one: report two-qubit gate count and depth after transpilation, with a fixed seed for reproducibility.

Going deeper

  • Optimal qubit mapping and routing is NP-hard in general, so production compilers use heuristics; SABRE (Li, Ding and Xie, 2019) is the default layout and routing method in Qiskit.
  • Connectivity differs by platform: IBM Eagle and Heron use a heavy-hex lattice (degree 2-3), IBM Nighthawk a square lattice with 218 couplers for 120 qubits, Google Willow a square grid, and trapped-ion systems all-to-all connectivity.
  • Native sets: IBM Heron {RZ, SX, X, CZ} plus optional fractional RX/RZZ; Quantinuum arbitrary-angle ZZ phase gates with single-qubit rotations; IonQ GPi, GPi2 and MS-type gates; neutral atoms global and local rotations plus Rydberg CZ.
  • Qiskit's preset pass managers use optimisation levels 0-3; level 3 adds heavier resynthesis (two-qubit KAK blocks, commutation analysis) at higher compile time, and the transpiler core has been largely rewritten in Rust for speed.
  • Noise-aware compilation uses calibration data to pick qubits and routes with lower error; VF2Layout searches for a perfect subgraph match before falling back to SABRE.
  • Other compilers include Quantinuum's TKET (pytket), Cirq's transformers, Berkeley Lab's BQSKit for numerical synthesis, and IBM's AI-assisted routing passes in the qiskit-ibm-transpiler package.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing algorithm performance using untranspiled gate counts, which can understate real costs several-fold.
  • Forgetting to fix seeds: stochastic layout and routing give different circuits on each run, confusing benchmarks.
  • Assuming all-to-all connectivity in algorithm designs meant for superconducting chips with nearest-neighbour couplings.

docs.title: Try it: Transpile for a line-connected 5-qubit device at two optimisation levels (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.providers.fake_provider import GenericBackendV2
from qiskit.transpiler import CouplingMap, generate_preset_pass_manager

backend = GenericBackendV2(num_qubits=5, basis_gates=['cz', 'rz', 'sx', 'x'],
                           coupling_map=CouplingMap.from_line(5), seed=1)
qc = QuantumCircuit(5); qc.h(0)
for t in range(1, 5):
    qc.cx(0, t)
for level in (0, 3):
    pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level=level, backend=backend, seed_transpiler=7)
    out = pm.run(qc)
    print(level, dict(out.count_ops()), 'depth', out.depth())

Level 0 is handy for debugging because it changes the circuit as little as possible. Gate cancellation and resynthesisOptimisation passes · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate Removing inverse pairs, merging rotations and rewriting two-qubit blocks optimally (KAK). CX·CX on the same qubits cancels to nothing; RZ(a)·RZ(b) merges into RZ(a + b). Scheduling and dynamical decouplingQiskit PadDynamicalDecoupling · Concept · Current · Advanced Assigning gate times and filling idle periods with echo pulses that cancel slow noise. Inserting X–X pulse pairs on idle qubits during a long CNOT ladder improved measured fidelity in IBM demonstrations. TKET (pytket)Quantinuum (open source) · Software · Current · Intermediate Retargetable compiler with strong routing and optimisation, supporting many hardware back-ends. A team compiles the same circuit with pytket for Quantinuum Helios and for IBM hardware via extensions. Cirq transformersGoogle Quantum AI · Software · Current · Intermediate Cirq's compilation functions for optimising circuits and converting them to device gate sets. cirq.optimize_for_target_gateset(circuit, gateset=cirq.CZTargetGateset()) rewrites a circuit for CZ hardware. BQSKitLawrence Berkeley National Laboratory · Software · Current · Advanced Berkeley Quantum Synthesis Toolkit: numerical, block-based synthesis that resynthesises circuit pieces optimally. Researchers use BQSKit to shrink CNOT counts of variational circuits beyond what rule-based passes find. AI-assisted transpilationIBM qiskit-ibm-transpiler AI passes · Tool · Emerging · Advanced Machine-learned routing and synthesis passes that can produce shorter circuits for large problems. IBM reported AI routing passes reducing two-qubit gate counts on many benchmark circuits versus standard heuristics.

docs.title: 2.13 Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (One-Way and Fusion-Based)
docs.text:
Measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) turns the usual recipe upside down. You first build a large entangled 'resource' state, called a cluster state, and then compute purely by measuring its qubits one by one, choosing each measurement angle based on earlier results. It is as powerful as the circuit model and is especially natural for photonic quantum computers.

A small cluster state as a one-way computer. Edges are CZ bonds; measuring left to right pushes the logical qubit along the chain.

Think of it like…

MBQC is like carving a sculpture from a block of marble: the entangled block is prepared first, and the computation is the pattern of chisel strokes (measurements) you choose — each stroke depending on how the last one went.

Real-world example

Inés programs a photonic machine at the fictional Lumen Photonics. Instead of applying gates, her compiler converts a circuit into a pattern of single-photon measurement angles on a stream of entangled photons. When an earlier measurement returns 1, the controller flips the sign of a later angle within nanoseconds, correcting the random 'byproduct' so the logical computation stays on track.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Prepare qubits in |+⟩ and apply CZ along the edges of a graph, creating a cluster (graph) state.
  2. Measure the first column of qubits in rotated bases; each angle encodes a gate.
  3. Each outcome teleports the logical state one step along, with a known Pauli 'byproduct'.
  4. Feed outcomes forward: adapt later measurement angles (e.g., θ → −θ) to cancel byproducts.
  5. Read the output from the final unmeasured qubits, applying any remaining Pauli corrections classically.

Who uses it

Photonic hardware companies, quantum-network researchers and fault-tolerance architects working on fusion-based schemes use MBQC.

Key takeaway

Key fact: a 2D cluster state plus adaptive single-qubit measurements is universal; the entangling work is done up front, and all the computing is measurement plus classical feed-forward.

Going deeper

  • Raussendorf and Briegel introduced the one-way quantum computer in 2001; any circuit maps to a measurement pattern on a 2D cluster state with polynomial overhead.
  • Measuring a cluster qubit in the basis (|0⟩ ± e^(iθ)|1⟩)/√2 applies H·RZ(−θ) to the next qubit up to a Pauli X^m byproduct, so a chain of measurements composes arbitrary single-qubit rotations.
  • Measurements in the Pauli bases (X, Y, Z) implement Clifford parts and can all be done at once at the start, leaving only non-Clifford angles adaptive — a big help for timing.
  • Fusion-based quantum computing (PsiQuantum, Bartolucci et al., 2021-2023) builds large resource states by 'fusing' small entangled photon states with two-photon measurements, tolerating photon loss by design.
  • Continuous-variable cluster states with time-multiplexed light pulses have reached very large mode counts — about one million modes in a 1D cluster (Tokyo, 2016) and 2D clusters in 2019 — though with limited squeezing quality.
  • Blind quantum computing (Broadbent, Fitzsimons and Kashefi, 2009) uses MBQC so a client can have a remote server run a computation without the server learning the input, output or algorithm.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking MBQC is a weaker 'measurement-only' model: with a suitable cluster state and feed-forward it is fully universal.
  • Ignoring feed-forward timing: adaptive angles must be updated faster than photons arrive or qubits decohere.
  • Assuming cluster states must exist all at once: photonic schemes create and consume them on the fly, slice by slice.

docs.title: Try it: One step of a one-way computer: a 2-qubit cluster turns a measurement angle into a gate (Qiskit 2.x)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

theta = 0.9
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.ry(0.7, 0)                 # input state |psi> on q0
qc.h(1)                       # q1 starts in |+>
qc.cz(0, 1)                   # one cluster bond
qc.rz(-theta, 0); qc.h(0)     # measure q0 in a basis rotated by theta
out = Statevector(qc).data.reshape(2, 2)[:, 0]   # keep runs where q0 gave 0
out /= np.linalg.norm(out)
ref = QuantumCircuit(1); ref.ry(0.7, 0); ref.rz(-theta, 0); ref.h(0)
print(abs(np.vdot(Statevector(ref).data, out))**2)  # 1.0: q1 = H.RZ(-theta)|psi>

docs.title: 2.14 Alternative Models: Adiabatic Quantum Computing, Quantum Annealing and Analog Simulation
docs.text:
Not all quantum computers run gate circuits. In adiabatic quantum computing you start a system in the easy-to-prepare lowest-energy state of a simple Hamiltonian and slowly morph it into a Hamiltonian whose lowest-energy state encodes your answer; if you go slowly enough, the system stays in the lowest state. Quantum annealers, such as D-Wave's, run a noisy, heuristic version of this for optimisation problems, and analog simulators directly mimic physical models.

Three ways to compute with quantum systems

Gate model Adiabatic QC Quantum annealing Program is Gate sequence Slow Hamiltonian sweep Ising/QUBO + schedule Universal? Yes Yes (in principle) No Error correction Well developed Limited theory Not available Typical hardware IBM, Google, Quantinuum Research only D-Wave Advantage2 Scale (2025) ~100-1,000 qubits Small experiments 4,400+ qubits Proven speed-up Yes (e.g. Shor) Equal to gate model None in general

Only the gate model and ideal adiabatic QC are proven universal; annealers are specialised optimisers.

Think of it like…

Adiabatic computing is like carrying a sleeping baby from the sofa to the cot: move smoothly and slowly and the baby (system) stays asleep (in the ground state); rush it and the baby wakes up (jumps to an excited state, giving a wrong answer).

Real-world example

Priyanka, an analyst at the fictional Meridian Freight, encodes a small truck-to-depot assignment as a QUBO with 300 binary variables and submits it to a D-Wave Advantage2 system through the Leap cloud. The annealer returns 1,000 samples in well under a second of QPU time. She then compares the best sample against a classical solver — a step any honest evaluation must include.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Encode the problem as an Ising or QUBO energy function whose minimum is the answer.
  2. Start in the ground state of a driver Hamiltonian, e.g. −Σ X_i, whose ground state is |+…+⟩.
  3. Slowly interpolate H(s) = (1 − s)·H_driver + s·H_problem as s goes from 0 to 1.
  4. If the change is slow relative to 1/gap² (the minimum energy gap), the system ends in the problem's ground state.
  5. Read out all qubits; repeat many times and keep the lowest-energy samples.

Who uses it

Optimisation researchers, operations-research teams piloting annealers, and condensed-matter physicists using analog simulators work with these models.

Key takeaway

Know the distinction: ideal adiabatic QC is universal and equivalent to the circuit model; commercial quantum annealing is a non-universal, heuristic optimiser with no proven general speed-up.

Going deeper

  • The adiabatic theorem (Born and Fock, 1928) guarantees staying in the ground state if evolution time scales roughly as 1/Δ², where Δ is the minimum spectral gap; exponentially small gaps mean exponentially long runs.
  • Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Sipser proposed adiabatic quantum computation in 2000; Aharonov, van Dam, Kempe, Landau, Lloyd and Regev proved it polynomially equivalent to the circuit model (2004, published 2007).
  • Kadowaki and Nishimori proposed quantum annealing in 1998; D-Wave sold the first commercial annealer (D-Wave One, 128 qubits) in 2011, and Advantage2 became generally available in May 2025 with 4,400+ qubits and 20-way Zephyr connectivity.
  • Problems must be minor-embedded onto the annealer's hardware graph, with chains of physical qubits representing one logical variable; chains reduce usable problem size and can break.
  • D-Wave and collaborators reported in Science (March 2025) a quantum simulation of magnetic-material dynamics they described as beyond classical; several groups replied with classical tensor-network simulations, so the claim remains debated.
  • Analog quantum simulators — such as neutral-atom arrays operated in analog mode (QuEra's 256-atom Aquila on Amazon Braket) — directly realise spin models to study phases of matter rather than running general programs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating annealer qubit counts as comparable to gate-model qubits: they are different, non-universal devices.
  • Accepting optimisation speed-up claims without comparison to state-of-the-art classical solvers such as Gurobi or simulated annealing.
  • Thinking 'slower is always better' on real hardware: long anneals suffer more from noise and thermal excitation.

docs.title: Try it: Simulate adiabatic evolution on 3 qubits: slower anneals find the ground state (NumPy + SciPy)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm

n = 3
X, I2 = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]), np.eye(2)
def on(k):                                   # X acting on qubit k of n
    m = np.array([[1.0]])
    for j in range(n):
        m = np.kron(m, X if j == k else I2)
    return m
H0 = -sum(on(k) for k in range(n))           # easy start: ground state |+++>
E = np.array([3, 1, 2, 0.5, 2, 1.5, -1, 2.5])  # problem energies; 110 is lowest
HP = np.diag(E)
for T in (1, 10, 100):                       # total anneal time
    psi, steps = np.ones(8) / np.sqrt(8), 200
    for k in range(steps):
        s = (k + 0.5) / steps                # schedule s: 0 -> 1
        psi = expm(-1j * (T / steps) * ((1 - s) * H0 + s * HP)) @ psi
    print(f"T={T:>3}: P(ground state 110) = {abs(psi[6])**2:.3f}")

docs.text: Name What it does Example Adiabatic theoremMax Born and Vladimir Fock, 1928 · Principle · Intermediate A system evolving slowly enough stays in its instantaneous ground state if a gap separates it from excited states. Halving the minimum gap requires roughly four times longer evolution to keep the same success rate. Adiabatic quantum computing (AQC)Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Sipser, 2000 · Concept · Research · Intermediate Computing by slowly morphing a simple Hamiltonian into one whose ground state encodes the answer. An AQC solver for 3-SAT encodes each violated clause as an energy penalty in the final Hamiltonian. AQC-circuit equivalenceAharonov, van Dam, Kempe, Landau, Lloyd and Regev, 2004/2007 · Milestone · Current · Advanced Proof that ideal adiabatic quantum computation and the circuit model can simulate each other with polynomial overhead. This result means AQC is universal in principle, though its fault-tolerance theory is far less developed. Spectral gapHamiltonian spectrum · Metric · Advanced Energy difference between ground and first excited states during the sweep; small gaps force slow, long anneals. Some hard optimisation instances have gaps shrinking exponentially with size, killing adiabatic speed-ups. Ising model and QUBOPhysics / operations research · Math · Current · Beginner Energy functions over ±1 spins or 0/1 bits with linear and pairwise terms; the input format for annealers. Minimise x1 + x2 − 2·x1·x2 + 3·x3: a QUBO with 3 binary variables and one pairwise term. Quantum annealingKadowaki and Nishimori, 1998 · Concept · Current · Beginner Heuristic optimisation that uses a decreasing transverse field to help a spin system find low-energy states. A scheduling team samples thousands of low-energy assignments from an annealer, then refines the best classically. D-Wave Advantage2D-Wave Quantum Inc., GA May 2025 · Platform · Current · Beginner Superconducting quantum annealer with 4,400+ qubits, 40,000+ couplers and 20-way Zephyr connectivity, via Leap cloud or on-premises. Users submit problems through D-Wave's Ocean SDK and receive samples within milliseconds of QPU access time. Minor embeddingD-Wave Ocean (minorminer) · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate Mapping a problem graph onto the hardware graph by chaining physical qubits to represent one variable. A fully connected 100-variable problem may need chains of several qubits per variable on the Zephyr graph. Transverse-field Ising HamiltonianCondensed-matter physics · Math · Advanced H = −A(s)·Σ X_i + B(s)·(Σ h_i Z_i + Σ J_ij Z_i Z_j): the Hamiltonian annealers physically implement. At s = 0 the X term dominates (all qubits in |+⟩); at s = 1 only the problem's Z terms remain. A logistics team seeds the annealer with a classical solver's route and explores improved neighbours. Standard transverse-field annealing is stoquastic, one reason proven speed-ups have been hard to find. Within days, independent teams posted classical simulations of parts of the problem, showing how advantage claims get tested. QuEra's 256-atom Aquila on Amazon Braket lets users program Rydberg-atom positions and laser sweeps to study phases. A depth-1 QAOA for MaxCut on a 20-node graph uses one RZZ layer and one RX layer, tuned by two angles.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Quantum Hardware & Qubit Technologies
docs.text: This chapter opens the box: what physically counts as a qubit, and how companies build machines from superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons, silicon spins, topological wires and more. It covers the refrigerators, vacuum systems, lasers and control electronics that make qubits work, the numbers used to judge hardware, and the 2026-2030 roadmaps — with a sceptic's toolkit for reading them.

docs.title: 4.1 What Makes a Good Qubit: DiVincenzo Criteria and Modalities
docs.text:
In 2000 David DiVincenzo listed five requirements any quantum computer must meet, plus two more for quantum communication. Every hardware platform — superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons, spins in silicon — is a different trade-off against these criteria, and as of 2026 no single platform has won.

Three leading modalities at a glance (2026)

Superconducting Trapped ion Neutral atom Qubit Josephson-junction circuit Internal levels of an ion Internal levels of an atom Environment ~10 mK dilution fridge Ultra-high vacuum, lasers Ultra-high vacuum, laser tweezers Two-qubit gate time ~20-300 ns ~10-500 µs ~0.2-1 µs (plus slow moves) Best two-qubit fidelity ~99.7-99.9% ~99.9-99.99% ~99.5%+ Connectivity Nearest neighbour on chip All-to-all in a module Reconfigurable by moving atoms Scale in 2026 ~100-160 per chip ~100 per system 1,000-6,000 trapped atoms

Each platform wins on different rows; typical values, not records.

Think of it like…

Choosing a qubit technology is like choosing a material for a bridge: steel, concrete and timber all carry loads, but each trades strength, cost, speed of construction and maintenance differently.

Real-world example

Lina, founder of the fictional start-up Qubitline, compares platforms for a chemistry product. Superconducting qubits run two-qubit gates in tens of nanoseconds but need 10 mK refrigerators; trapped ions reach 99.9%+ fidelity with all-to-all links but gates take tens to hundreds of microseconds; neutral atoms scale to thousands of qubits but cycle more slowly. She picks partners for each stage of her roadmap.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A scalable physical system with well-characterised qubits.
  2. The ability to initialise qubits to a simple state such as |00…0⟩.
  3. Coherence times much longer than gate times.
  4. A universal set of quantum gates.
  5. Qubit-specific measurement.
  6. For networking: convert between stationary and flying (photonic) qubits.
  7. For networking: transmit flying qubits faithfully between locations.

Who uses it

Hardware engineers, physicists, investors and product managers comparing technologies; it is a standard interview and exam question.

Key takeaway

Memorise '5 + 2' criteria and the key figure of merit: coherence time divided by gate time — e.g. 100 µs / 50 ns ≈ 2,000 operations before the qubit forgets.

Going deeper

  • DiVincenzo's criteria appeared in 'The Physical Implementation of Quantum Computation' (Fortschritte der Physik, 2000); the two networking criteria anticipate today's modular and distributed architectures.
  • Modern additions to the list include connectivity, crosstalk, leakage out of the qubit subspace, fabrication yield, control-wiring scalability, speed of the error-correction cycle and compatibility with a practical code.
  • Natural qubits (ions, atoms) are identical by physics, so no two differ; fabricated qubits (superconducting, spins) vary from device to device and need individual calibration and frequency allocation.
  • Speed matters for useful runtime: an error-correction cycle of about 1 µs (superconducting) versus about 1 ms (ions, atoms) means a thousand-fold difference in wall-clock time unless slow platforms parallelise more.
  • As of 2026 the DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative's Stage B spans superconducting (IBM, Nord Quantique), ions (IonQ, Quantinuum), atoms (Atom Computing, QuEra), spins (Diraq, Quantum Motion, SQC) and photonics (Xanadu, Photonic Inc.).
  • Stationary-to-flying conversion is hardest for superconducting qubits, whose microwave photons cannot travel through room-temperature fibre; microwave-to-optical transducers remain inefficient research devices.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing raw qubit counts across modalities: 1,000 trapped atoms and 156 superconducting qubits differ hugely in speed, fidelity and connectivity.
  • Judging a platform by one number such as coherence time; what matters is coherence relative to gate time, plus fidelity and scalability.
  • Assuming the 'winner' is already decided; companies and DARPA are still funding five or more modalities in parallel.

docs.title: Try it: Rough 'operations per coherence time' for typical 2025-26 devices
docs.text:
devices = {  # (typical T2 in seconds, typical two-qubit gate time in seconds) - rough orders of magnitude
    'transmon':     (150e-6, 60e-9),
    'trapped ion':  (1.0,    200e-6),
    'neutral atom': (1.0,    0.5e-6),   # but atom moves and readout take ~0.1-1 ms
}
for name, (t2, tg) in devices.items():
    print(f'{name:13s} ~{t2 / tg:,.0f} gate times per T2')

docs.title: Key concepts, algorithms, hardware, tools & milestones
docs.text: Name What it does Example DiVincenzo criteriaDavid DiVincenzo, IBM (2000) · Principle · Current · Beginner Five requirements for a quantum computer plus two for quantum communication, used to assess any qubit technology. An exam asks students to score photonic qubits against each criterion, noting weak point 4 (two-qubit gates). Qubit modalityHardware taxonomy · Concept · Current · Beginner The physical system storing a qubit: superconducting circuit, ion, atom, photon, electron spin, defect or topological mode. Analyst reports group companies by modality before comparing roadmaps and funding. Scalable, well-characterised qubitsDiVincenzo criterion 1 · Concept · Current · Beginner Qubits whose physics is understood well enough to model errors, and that can be multiplied without redesign. Neutral atoms score well on scaling, with 6,100 trapped in one array, but characterising every site is still demanding. Initialisation and resetDiVincenzo criterion 2 · Concept · Current · Beginner Preparing every qubit in a known starting state, and resetting quickly mid-circuit for error correction. Ions are reset by optical pumping in microseconds; transmons use active reset pulses instead of waiting several T1 times. Coherence-to-gate-time ratioDiVincenzo criterion 3 · Metric · Current · Beginner How many operations fit within a qubit's coherence time; a quick figure of merit across platforms. A transmon with T2 = 100 µs and 50 ns gates allows about 2,000 gate times before dephasing dominates. Vendor native gate setsDiVincenzo criterion 4, vendor specific · Concept · Current · Intermediate Each platform physically implements a different small gate set, chosen to suit its physics; all else is compiled into it. IBM Heron uses CZ, RZ, SX and X; Quantinuum uses arbitrary-angle ZZ and single-qubit rotations; IonQ uses MS/ZZ-type gates. Qubit-specific readoutDiVincenzo criterion 5 · Concept · Current · Beginner Measuring each qubit individually without disturbing neighbours, ideally fast and mid-circuit. Ions are read by shining a laser and counting fluorescence photons on a camera; dark means |1⟩, bright means |0⟩ (or vice versa). Stationary vs flying qubitsDiVincenzo criteria 6-7 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Stationary qubits compute and store; flying qubits, almost always photons, carry quantum information between modules. Trapped-ion modules are linked by entangling each ion with an emitted photon and interfering the photons. Microwave-to-optical transductionResearch area · Concept · Research · Advanced Converting a superconducting qubit's microwave photon into an optical photon for fibre links; efficiencies remain low. Groups use piezo-optomechanical or electro-optic devices, but efficiency and added noise remain far from what networking requires. Fabrication yield and variabilityManufactured qubits · Concept · Current · Intermediate Fabricated qubits differ slightly in frequency and coherence, and some fail; yield decides how large a working chip can be. IBM's 1,121-qubit Condor was partly a test of whether fabrication and packaging yield hold up at four-digit qubit counts. CrosstalkError type · Concept · Current · Intermediate Unwanted interaction where driving or measuring one qubit disturbs another, often worse when many operate simultaneously. Benchmarks report 'simultaneous' gate errors because isolated-pair numbers hide crosstalk. Modular architectureScaling strategy · Concept · Emerging · Intermediate Building large machines from many smaller modules linked by couplers or photonic interconnects. IBM's roadmap links Kookaburra modules with on-chip and inter-chip couplers; IonQ and Quantinuum plan photonic links.

docs.title: 4.2 Superconducting Qubits: Transmons, Fluxonium and Couplers
docs.text:
Superconducting qubits are tiny electrical circuits on a chip, made from metals such as aluminium, niobium or tantalum and cooled to about 10 millikelvin so current flows without resistance. A Josephson junction makes the circuit's energy levels unevenly spaced, so its two lowest levels can be used as a qubit and controlled with microwave pulses.

Around one transmon on a chip. Each qubit needs a drive path, a coupler to its neighbours and a readout chain.

Think of it like…

A transmon is like a guitar string tuned so the overtones are slightly out of step: you can pluck the first note cleanly without accidentally sounding the next one. The Josephson junction is the clever fret that makes the spacing uneven.

Real-world example

Carla, a hardware engineer at the fictional Northlight Quantum, characterises a new transmon: frequency 4.8 GHz, anharmonicity −220 MHz, T1 = 120 µs and echo T2 = 150 µs. A 25 ns single-qubit pulse shaped with DRAG reaches 99.95% fidelity, and a tunable coupler lets her switch the interaction with its neighbour on and off.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A Josephson junction (Al / aluminium oxide / Al) plus a capacitor forms a nonlinear oscillator.
  2. The two lowest levels, typically 4-6 GHz apart for a transmon, become |0⟩ and |1⟩.
  3. Shaped microwave pulses on a drive line rotate the qubit; DRAG shaping avoids leaking into |2⟩.
  4. Two-qubit gates use couplers: tunable-coupler CZ, cross-resonance or parametric iSWAP-type gates.
  5. Dispersive readout: a resonator's frequency shifts with the qubit state; the weak signal is boosted by a quantum-limited amplifier and a HEMT.

Who uses it

Device physicists, microwave engineers, fabrication and materials scientists at IBM, Google, Rigetti, IQM, AWS and many start-ups and universities.

Key takeaway

Transmon = charge-insensitive (E_J/E_C ≈ 50 or more) at the cost of small anharmonicity (about −200 to −300 MHz); fluxonium = lower frequency and larger anharmonicity, holding the superconducting single-qubit fidelity record of 99.998% (MIT, 2025).

Going deeper

  • The transmon (Koch et al., Yale, 2007) shunts the junction with a large capacitor so E_J/E_C ≳ 50, making charge noise exponentially weak; at about 5 GHz the thermal excited population at 10-20 mK is negligible.
  • Fluxonium (Manucharyan et al., 2009) adds a 'superinductor' of many junctions, giving qubit frequencies of hundreds of MHz, large anharmonicity and long T1; MIT reported 99.92% two-qubit and 99.998% single-qubit fidelities.
  • Coherence is limited mainly by two-level-system defects in surface oxides and interfaces; tantalum films on sapphire pushed T1 to about 0.3 ms (2021), and Aalto reported T1 up to about 0.67 ms and echo T2 above 1 ms (2025).
  • Two-qubit gate families: cross-resonance or echoed cross-resonance (older IBM Falcon and Eagle), tunable-coupler CZ (IBM Heron, Google), iSWAP-like fSim gates (Google RCS) and parametric gates (Rigetti); durations of roughly 20-300 ns.
  • Readout takes a few hundred nanoseconds to about 1 µs using a dispersively coupled resonator, a Josephson parametric or travelling-wave amplifier, and a HEMT amplifier at 4 K.
  • Correlated errors from cosmic rays and natural radioactivity create bursts of quasiparticles affecting many qubits at once (McEwen et al., Nature Physics 2022); gap engineering and shielding mitigate them.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing these with room-temperature superconductors: the metals superconduct only near absolute zero, and qubits additionally need millikelvin temperatures.
  • Judging qubit quality by T1 alone; two-qubit gate fidelity, readout error, leakage and crosstalk matter just as much.
  • Forgetting frequency crowding: on large chips neighbouring qubits must avoid collisions, which complicates fabrication and calibration.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate a transmon's frequency and anharmonicity from E_J and E_C
docs.text:
import numpy as np
EJ, EC = 15.0, 0.25                 # GHz; EJ/EC = 60 is typical for a transmon
f01 = np.sqrt(8 * EJ * EC) - EC     # qubit transition frequency
alpha = -EC                         # anharmonicity f12 - f01
print(f'f01 = {f01:.2f} GHz, f12 = {f01 + alpha:.2f} GHz, anharmonicity = {alpha*1000:.0f} MHz')
# f01 = 5.23 GHz, f12 = 4.98 GHz, anharmonicity = -250 MHz

docs.title: Key concepts, algorithms, hardware, tools & milestones
docs.text: Name What it does Example Josephson junctionBrian Josephson (1962); Al/AlOx/Al fabrication · Hardware · Current · Beginner Two superconductors separated by a thin insulator; its nonlinear inductance makes qubit energy levels unequally spaced. A junction about 100 nm across is made by double-angle shadow evaporation of aluminium. TransmonKoch et al., Yale (2007) · Qubit type · Current · Beginner A Josephson junction shunted by a large capacitor; the dominant superconducting qubit, insensitive to charge noise. IBM Heron and Google Willow both use transmon qubits at about 4-6 GHz. FluxoniumManucharyan, Koch, Glazman & Devoret (2009) · Qubit type · Emerging · Intermediate A junction shunted by a superinductor; low frequency, large anharmonicity and long T1, with record gate fidelities. MIT's 2025 fluxonium experiments reached 99.998% single-qubit fidelity using fast, carefully shaped pulses. AnharmonicityTransmon physics · Concept · Current · Intermediate The difference between the 1→2 and 0→1 transition frequencies; it lets pulses address only the qubit levels. With −250 MHz anharmonicity, pulses shorter than about 10 ns start exciting |2⟩ unless shaped. Tunable couplerGoogle Sycamore; IBM Heron; IQM; Rigetti · Hardware · Current · Intermediate An extra circuit element whose frequency is adjusted to switch qubit-qubit interaction on for gates and off otherwise. IBM's Nighthawk links 120 qubits with 218 tunable couplers in a square lattice. Cross-resonance gateRigetti & Devoret (2010); Chow et al., IBM (2011) · Gate · Legacy · Advanced Driving one fixed-frequency qubit at its neighbour's frequency to create a ZX interaction, the basis of IBM's ECR gate. IBM Eagle processors used echoed cross-resonance (ECR) as their native two-qubit gate. Dispersive readoutCircuit quantum electrodynamics (Blais et al., 2004) · Concept · Current · Intermediate A resonator coupled to the qubit shifts frequency depending on the qubit state; probing it reveals 0 or 1. A 300 ns readout pulse at 7 GHz distinguishes the two states with about 99% assignment fidelity. Josephson parametric amplifier / TWPASuperconducting quantum-limited amplifiers · Hardware · Current · Advanced Amplifiers adding close to the minimum noise allowed by quantum mechanics, the first stage of qubit readout. A travelling-wave parametric amplifier boosts readout signals of a whole chip over several GHz of bandwidth. DRAG pulse shapingMotzoi, Gambetta, Rebentrost & Wilhelm (2009) · Concept · Current · Advanced Adds a derivative-shaped quadrature component to pulses to suppress leakage and phase errors in weakly anharmonic qubits. Calibrating the DRAG coefficient sharply reduces a 20 ns X gate's leakage into |2⟩ and its phase error. Two-level-system (TLS) defectsMaterials science · Concept · Current · Advanced Microscopic defects in oxides and interfaces that absorb qubit energy and fluctuate over time, limiting T1. A qubit's T1 drops from 200 µs to 40 µs overnight when a TLS drifts into resonance with it. Tantalum-based qubitsPlace et al., Nature Communications (2021) · Hardware · Emerging · Advanced Transmons with tantalum films on sapphire, whose cleaner oxides cut TLS losses and raised T1 toward 0.3-0.5 ms. Several labs switched from niobium to tantalum capacitor pads to roughly double coherence. Quasiparticle and cosmic-ray burstsMcEwen et al., Nature Physics (2022) · Concept · Current · Advanced High-energy particle impacts break Cooper pairs across the chip, causing correlated errors that error correction struggles with. Google observed chip-wide error bursts about every 10 seconds before redesigning chips to resist them.

docs.title: 4.3 Superconducting Processors in 2026: IBM, Google, Rigetti, IQM and More
docs.text:
Superconducting qubits are the most widely deployed gate-model technology, used by IBM, Google, Rigetti, IQM, China's USTC, Fujitsu and RIKEN, AWS and others. This section maps the actual chips available or announced by 2026 and what each one demonstrates.

Qubits per superconducting processor. IBM's 1,121-qubit Condor was a scaling test; today's best-performing chips hold 100-160 qubits.

Think of it like…

It is like a smartphone chip line-up: every vendor releases generations that trade core count (qubits), wiring (connectivity) and error rates, and the newest is not always best for every job.

Real-world example

Tomás, a graduate student, compares IBM's Heron r3 device ibm_boston (156 qubits, best 100-qubit EPLG about 0.2%) with the newer Nighthawk ibm_miami (120 qubits on a square lattice, early access in 2026). He then reads Google's Willow spec sheet: 105 qubits, mean CZ error 0.33% on the error-correction chip, 1.1 µs surface-code cycle.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Design the qubit lattice: IBM heavy-hex (degree 2-3), square lattices (degree 4) at Google, IBM Nighthawk and IQM.
  2. Fabricate multi-layer chips: qubit layer, wiring layers and bump bonds or through-silicon vias for signals.
  3. Package the chip and mount it on the mixing-chamber plate of a dilution refrigerator.
  4. Calibrate frequencies, pulses and couplers, typically at least daily.
  5. Benchmark with randomised benchmarking, layer fidelity or XEB, and publish the numbers.
  6. Expose the device through a cloud platform with a transpiler that knows its native gates and connectivity.

Who uses it

Quantum software developers choosing backends, hardware analysts, and engineers at IBM, Google Quantum AI, Rigetti, IQM, Fujitsu, AWS and national labs.

Key takeaway

Memorise: IBM Heron (133/156 qubits, heavy-hex, tunable couplers), IBM Nighthawk (120 qubits, 218 couplers, square lattice, 2025), Google Willow (105 qubits, December 2024), Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q (generally available April 2026), Zuchongzhi 3.0 (105 qubits, 2025).

Going deeper

  • IBM's line: Eagle (127, 2021), Osprey (433, 2022), Condor (1,121, 2023) and Heron r1 (133, 2023), r2 (156, 2024) and r3 (2025, e.g. ibm_pittsburgh and ibm_boston, best 100-qubit EPLG about 2.2×10⁻³).
  • IBM Nighthawk (announced November 2025, cloud early access from early 2026 as ibm_miami): 120 qubits, 218 tunable couplers on a square lattice, about 30% more complex circuits than Heron; IBM targets 7,500 two-qubit gates by end-2026 and 10,000 in 2027.
  • IBM Loon (2025) is an experimental processor testing qLDPC error-correction ingredients: long-range on-chip 'c-couplers', multi-layer routing and fast qubit reset.
  • Google Willow (December 2024): 105 qubits, average connectivity 3.47; the error-correction chip has mean CZ error 0.33%, readout error 0.77%, T1 about 68 µs and Λ = 2.14; the RCS chip has T1 about 98 µs and 0.14% iSWAP-like error.
  • Rigetti uses chiplets: Ankaa-3 (84 qubits, December 2024), Cepheus-1-36Q (four 9-qubit chiplets, 2025) and Cepheus-1-108Q (twelve chiplets, April 2026, 99.1% median two-qubit fidelity at launch, 99.5% targeted).
  • Others: IQM Radiance on-premises systems of 20, 54 or 150 qubits (150-qubit deliveries planned for 2026), Fujitsu and RIKEN's 256-qubit machine (2025), USTC's Zuchongzhi 3.0 (99.62% two-qubit fidelity), and D-Wave's 2026 move into gate models via Quantum Circuits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing a backend by qubit count: a 156-qubit device with lower errors beats a larger noisy one for almost every algorithm.
  • Trusting spec sheets for today's run: calibrations drift daily, so check the live properties of the device before submitting jobs.
  • Treating 'best pair' or 'best layer' numbers as typical; medians and full distributions describe what your circuit will meet.
